speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg to lay on the table a copy of the order in council appointing a royal commission to inquire into and report on the penal system of Canada.
Civil Service Act

Mr. OSCAR L. BOULANGER (Belle-chasse) moved for leave to introduce Bill No.
8,	to amend the Post Office Act.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, I think the best way to explain the object of the bill will be for me to read the explanatory note. It is as follows:
The object of this bill is to abolish the obsolete and unsatisfactory system of awarding by tender contracts for the transportation of mail. Moreover, everyone knows that the principle of awarding mail contracts by tender and to the lowest tenderer has been more often disregarded than observed'. It is sought by this bill to establish a more open and honest practice and at the same time allow the Postmaster General properly to remunerate the mail carriers who perform the important function of transporting the mail of Canada.
As the house will have observed, the object of the bill is to do away with the present system of awarding mail contracts by tender. The bill proposes, instead of the old system, to establish a system of awarding contracts at the discretion of the Postmaster General when the contract does not exceed $1,000, and at the discretion of the governor general in council when the contract is over $1,000, without tender and at a flat rate.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. OSCAR L. BOULANGER (Belie-chasse) moved for leave to introduce Bill No.
9,	to amend the Civil Service Act (vacancies, outside service, priority to returned soldiers).
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, this bill has four objects in view. The first is to place the outside civil service outside the control of the civil service commission. Secondly, the bill proposes that it shall be obligatory for the civil service commission to consult the heads of departments before making appointments or promotions in order that the last word in making appointments and promotions may be with heads of departments, and not with the commission. Thirdly, the bill proposes to restrict to Canadian veterans the preference granted to veterans by the Civil Service Act. Lastly, the bill proposes that it shall be obligatory for the civil service commission, whenever they desire to appoint to a position in the civil service a candidate who has not resided five years in Canada, to bring the appointment before the cabinet. At the present time there is a blanket order in council and a regulation of the civil service com-
JMr. Lapointe.]
mission which authorize the commission in certain cases to appoint to the civil service a person who has not had the necessary five years' residence in Canada. The bill proposes that in future it will be necessary for the civil service commission, whenever they feel the necessity of overriding the Civil Service Act in that respect, to come before the government and state the special reasons which necessitate such an appointment.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

PROrOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King:

Canada-TJ3. Trade Agreement
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the trade agreement entered into at Washington on the 15th day of November, 1935, between His Majesty's government in the Dominion of Canada and the government of the United States of America, and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I think it perhaps desirable
to correct some misapprehensions of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as indicated in his address the other day, before I deal more specifically with the provisions of the agreement which is now before the house for consideration. I do not desire to do this at any great length, nor would I bother the house were it not for the fact that, by not dealing with them, it might seem that I had accepted them as being a correct statement of the situation.
It is not correct to say that the Liberal party during all its existence has supported reciprocity, nor is it correct to say that the Conservative party has in any sense opposed it. I find, by reference to the statutes of 1868, that in the first statute dealing with such matters and enacted by this parliament provision was made whereby a standing offer to the United States was embodied in the statute, dealing with natural products; and later on, in 1879, when the national policy was introduced, provision was definitely made by which a statutory offer was extended to the United States. In order that there may be no misunderstanding with respect to that, it might perhaps be desirable to read the resolution upon which the statute was founded. It was resolution No. 5 and was submitted to the house by Sir Leonard Tilley on March 14, 1879:
That it is expedient to provide that any or all of the following articles, that is to say:- Animals of all kinds, green fruit, hay, straw, bran, seeds of all kinds, vegetables (including potatoes and other roots), plants, trees and shrubs, coal and coke, salt, hops, wheat, peas and beans, barley, rye, oats, Indian corn, buckwheat, and all other grain, flour of wheat and flour of rye, Indian meal and oatmeal and flour or meal of any other grain, butter, cheese, fish (salted or smoked), lard, tallow, meat (fresh, salted or smoked), may be imported into Canada free of duty, or at a less rate of duty than is provided by this act, upon proclamation of the governor in council, which may be issued whenever it appears to his satisfaction that similar articles from Canada may be imported into the United States free of duty, or at a rate of duty not exceeding that payable on the same under such proclamation, when imported into Canada.
Upon that resolution a statute was founded, and in 1911, when the late Right Hon. W. S. Fielding was introducing his reciprocity resolutions and moving the house into committee of ways and means, he quoted that resolution as indicating the attitude of the Conservative party with respect to the matter of reciprocity.
I also take sharp issue with the Prime Minister when he contends that the so-called national policy was introduced as a retaliatory measure against the United States. I have only to refer to what was said by the Minister of Finance in introducing the budget on March 14, 1879, at pages 411 and 415 of Hansard of that day, to correct any possible misunderstanding. Discussing the question of giving more favourable treatment to goods from Great Britain than to goods from foreign countries, he said:
I think this house will not object if, in the propositions before me, they touch more heavily the imports from foreign countries than from our fatherland.... But the government couple with the proposal, in order to Show that we approach this question with no unfriendly spirit, a resolution that will be laid on the table containing a proposition to this effect: That, as to articles named, which are the natural products of the country, including lumber, if the United States take off the duties in part or in whole, we are prepared to meet them with equal concessions. The government believe in a reciprocity tariff, yet may discuss free trade or protection, but the question of to-day is-Shall we have a reciprocity tariff, or a one-sided' tariff? The government propose to do more.
And then Sir Charles Tupper said:
I believe within two years from the adoption of the national policy-not a policy of hostility to the United States, but one of following the system they had adopted to foster their industries-they will give us a free market for coal in the United States.
Further, Sir Leonard Tilley made clear the object to be attained by the tariff then introduced:
But if we undertake, as the present government have undertaken, to readjust and reorganize, and I may say, make an entirely new tariff, having for its object not only the realization of $2,000,000 more revenue than will he collected this year, but, in addition to providing for that deficiency, to adjust that policy, or that tariff with a view of making what has been, and is to-day, declared the policy of the majority of this house-I mean the protection of the industries of the country [DOT]-the magnitude of the undertaking will be the better appreciated.
These were the declarations made by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Railways of that day, Sir Leonard Tilley and Sir Charles Tupper, at the time the national policy became a part of the policy of this country, or at least the policy of the Conservative party, as it has been ever since.
I need hardly go further than to point out that every proposed reciprocity agreement that reached the point, shall I say, not
Canada-UJS. Trade Agreement

of being signed but of a consensus between the parties was brought forward while the Republican party was in office in the United States. In 1874, when George Brown negotiated with the United States, the Republican party was in office; in 1911 when the agreement was negotiated Mr. Taft was president -a Republican president. The recent agreement was of course negotiated with a Democratic president. I mention this because it is desirable that there Should be no misunderstanding with respect to the matter; for in the following years the United States expressed unwillingness to enter into agreements, as indicated a day or two ago; for in 1892 they declined to grant the concessions asked for by the government of that day, and in 1898, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier set up his joint high commission under the presidency of Lord Hersehell, they sat for nearly a solid year without results, and it was at that time that Sir Wilfrid Laurier made it perfectly clear that he did not propose longer to concern himself with an effort to negotiate a treaty with the United States. He said:
There will he no more pilgrimages to Washington. We are turning our hopes to the old motherland.
And what is more, not only did Sir Wilfrid say that but that is what he practised, and though in 1887 and 1891 the elections were contested on commercial union and unrestricted reciprocity, that was subsequently abandoned by the Liberal party. In consequence of the attitude taken by Mr. Blake and many others at that time, not only did he not go to the United States asking for further concessions after the joint high commission's failure, but he said he would not do it; and in 1911 it was not the action of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government that brought about the negotiations terminating in the proposals of 1911. I think it might be well to clear that up, because Mr. Fielding, in his letter to Mr. Knox, dwelt upon that point as one of some importance. He made it perfectly clear at that time that the initiative had come from the president of the day and not from himself or his government. The letter addressed to Mr. Knox-I will not read the whole of it, but it is important to keep it in mind-was dated at Washington on January 21, 1911:
Dear Mr. Secretary,-
The negotiations initiated by the president several months ago through your communication to his excellency the British ambassador respecting a reciprocal tariff arrangement between the United States and Canada, and since carried on directly between representatives of these two countries have now, we are

happy to say, reached a stage which gives reasonable assurance of a conclusion satisfactory to both countries.
Then follows this, after two intervening paragraphs:
The governments of the two countries having made this agreement from the conviction that, if confirmed by the necessary legislative authorities, it will benefit the people on, both sides of the border line, we may reasonably hope and expect that the arrangement, if so confirmed, will remain in operation for a considerable period. Only this expectation on the part of both governments would justify the time and labour that have been employed in the maturing of the proposed measures. Nevertheless, it is distinctly understood that we do not attempt to bind for the future the action of the United States Congress, or the Parliament of Canada, but that each of these authorities shall be absolutely free to make any change of tariff policy or of any other matter covered by the present arrangement that may be deemed expedient. We look for the continuance of the arrangement, not because either party is bound to it, but because of our conviction that the more liberal trade policy thus to be established will be viewed by the people of the United States and Canada as one which will strengthen the friendly relations now happily prevailing and promote the commercial interests of both countries.
That was a declaration by Mr. Fielding of the circumstances under which these negotiations were carried on. They failed because the Canadian people were not prepared to adopt them. The United States congress did approve them; but it must be within the memory of every member of this house that upon the very first opportunity afforded to the people of the United States to pass upon them they defeated them; the Republican administration was defeated at the polls and succeeded by the administration of Mr. Wilson. So that on the one hand you have the Canadian people rejecting the proposals, and on the other hand you have the United States people rejecting them at the first opportunity that was offered them so to do. That, I think, makes the record clear so far as that point is concerned, and there can be no misunderstanding, it seems to me, with respect to that part of the matter.
Let us now correct another misapprehension on the part of the right hon. gentleman, that is with respect to what took place after this government came into office. I wonder if for the moment the right hon. gentleman forgot that in June of 1930 the Hawley-Smoot tariff was enacted,-enacted despite the fact that in his place as prime minister he had asked this house and the country not to provoke them lest they do something more severe than that which they had done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Well, it is in Hansard. I can read it. Will somebody get me Hansard?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Read the whole of it. You misread it last time.

And that the British preference should not be increased lest per-adventure that might provoke the United States to further action. Those were the statements made by the right hon. gentleman in this house in 1930, about which there can be no possible doubt.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They are not.

They have been read too often for there to be any misunderstanding as to what they are.
That being so, let us analyze the next step with reference to it. There was in power in Washington in 1930 a Republican administration, and when the late government came into office it found Mr. Hoover the president of the United States, whose congress had just enacted the Hawley-Smoot tariff. But at the same time provision had been made whereby, in the event of its being concluded that an unfair tariff advantage was being given to the United States, application might be made to the tariff board for the purpose of securing if possible a report that the tariff was excessive, in which event the president was authorized to make a proclamation to reduce the tariff not beyond fifty per cent of what the existing tariff was. Many cases were heard by the tariff commission; amongst others, the tariff item with respect to maple sugar. When our minister went to the United States in 1931 he found, as I have said, a Republican administration in office, and his first effort, as the records of the department will show, was to bring to the attention of the American government the anomalies of their tariff as they affected cattle, hoping that an opportunity might be afforded before the tariff commission to deal with this matter in accordance with the provisions of the law to which I have referred. I personally know, as every member of this house probably knows from reading, that the president of the United States was not in accord with some of the provisions of the Hawley-Smoot tariff. He made it perfectly clear in public statements that he did not agree with them and that he was not unsympathetic to the suggestions made that we should endeavour to bring the matter before the tariff board. In fact an application was filed, but no action followed. During the whole of the period of office of President Hoover, namely during the year 1930, the remainder of the year after the late government came into office, the whole of the year 1931, the whole of the year 1932, and until March, 1933, the Hawley-Smoot tariff stood in its entirety and Mr. Hoover remained the president of the United States. And yet the right hon. gentleman asked the other day what the government was doing in 1931 and 1932 and 1933. Now I would ask him what he was doing from 1921 until 1930, dealing with Republican administrations under the same conditions. There need be no misapprehension, therefore, as to what the facts were, when the high tariffs of the Hawley-Smoot schedule still prevailed until 1933. But bear in mind, sir, they still continue; for there has been no legislation in the United States since 1933 dealing with the position of tariffs except through treaties or agreements made with various countries to which I shall presently refer.
Now that is important. There was not a change of government in the United States until March, 1933, and just as soon as that government came into office, as the records of the department of the Secretary of State will show, we pressed that there should be an adjustment of the tariff relations between the two countries. But the president, unwilling to open up the tariff schedules in congress, and unwilling as he was under the conditions that then prevailed to risk the possibility, nay the certainty of the United States senate rejeoting any tariff treaty that might be made, did what? He proposed legislation dealing with monetary problems, dealing with many other problems, with agriculture, many matters of the kind, and he then intimated that he proposed to have introduced into congress a measure affecting tariff questions, giving him executive authority to deal with those matters as he thought best, with such limitations as might be imposed upon his powers. In 1933 the measure was withdrawn; it was fiercely resisted, and it did not come into effect. Therefore the year 1933 went by with no legislation, but on June 12, 1934, the president signed the bill, which then became a statute, whereby executive power was conferred upon him by congress to make trade agreements with countries, subject first to there not being a greater reduction than fifty per cent, second that the period should be fixed at three years, and third that there should be no change from dutiable to free goods and, e converso, from free to dutiable; he had no such power. The last condition was that before he took this executive action he had to issue a proclamation indicating that he proposed to deal with whatever country was being dealt with, in order that those who might be
Canada-UJ3. Trade Agreement

interested should have an opportunity to present their objections, if they had any, to such an arrangement being made.
That was in June, 1934, and the records of the department will show that from the date that the act came into force, continuously until action was taken, there was constant communication between the department of state and the Canadian legation at Washington in an effort to have action taken in accordance with the provisions of the statute to which 1 have referred. It was ascertained very early, in fact it was known before, that it was a cardinal principle of any negotiations being entered into at all that the United States should receive from Canada or from any other country with which an agreement was made, an undertaking that the tariff concessions granted to the United States would be as great as those granted to any other country in the world, except in their own case with respect to their peninsular possessions and Cuba, with which country they had a special treaty arrangement. On our part we made it clear as a government that it was absolutely a sine qua non to the carrying on ol negotiations at all that the entire British preferences were to be untouched and that any negotiations carried on should be carried on not only subject to the provisions of those agreements but subject also to their future modification or extension.
That being so we embodied in a document our proposals for negotiation. At first the right hon. gentleman read the words as though he thought those were proposals, though I am frank to say that when attention was directed to it he modified his statement and said those were proposals for negotiation. So the proposals for negotiation were embodied in a note dated November, 1934, to which a reply was received in December and again the records of the department will show that efforts were being made constantly to induce action to be taken. But there was a reason why the president found it difficult to deal with some of these matters, a reason, I doubt not, that is in the minds of many members of the house at this moment. It was the fact that during the election campaign the president had made certain statements at Baltimore with respect to what he proposed to do in connection with agricultural commodities, and this was being constantly thrust upon his attention by those who were deeply interested in the maintenance of existing tariff legislation in connection with agricultural products. What were those words? On October 26, 1933, speaking during the election campaign at Baltimore, the president said:

My distinguished opponent is declaring in his speeches that I have proposed to injure or destroy the farmers' markets by reducing the tariff on products of the farm. That is silly. Of course I have made no such proposal, nor can any speech or statement I have made be so construed. I said in my Sioux City speech, in discussing the Ilawley-Smoot tariff act of 1930:
"Of course, the excessive, outrageously excessive rates in that bill must come down, but we should not lower them beyond the point indicated."
The point indicated was that no tariff duty should be lowered to a point where our natural industries would be injured....
Of course, it is absurd to talk of lowering tariff duties on farm products.... I know of no effective excessively high tariff duties on farm products. I do not intend that such duties shall be lowered. To do so would be inconsistent with my entire farm program, _ and every farmer knows it and will not be deceived.
That statement was being constantly presented to the attention of the president, and it made it increasingly difficult for the government of Canada, dealing with the question of negotiations on farm products, to make progress. Finally, however, in January, 1935, a proclamation was issued; interested parties were heard and the negotiations continued. Those negotiations were difficult by reason of the statement made by the president in connection with agricultural products; they were difficult because the very moment it was suggested that it was proposed to negotiate, a great body of public opinion crystallized against any such action being taken. Finally we did get certain preliminary discussions concluded. The matter of cattle, which was dealt with in a slightly different way than it is in the agreement now before us, lumber, whiskey and so on-* all these matters were early determined without difficulty, but when it came down to the question of what concessions the Dominion of Canada was to receive for the concessions that were sought the difficulty began. When I say to this house, as I presently shall, that we could not possibly agree to give the concessions that are given by this agreement for the slight concessions we were offered, I but state the simple truth, and I shall give the reasons why. In order that there may be no difficulty as to what was said by my right hon. friend in his speech in this house on April 9, 1929-speaking from memory I said 1930, but it was 1929-I quote from Hansard for that year:
Having that knowledge before us-
The right hon. gentleman was speaking of the knowledge they had of the situation.
-I ask hon. gentlemen irrespective of party: In the condition of prosperity which Canada is to-day enjoying would it be desirable on the part of the administration to take any action

Canada-TJjS. Trade Agreement
with respect to the tariff in Canada at the present time which by those across the line who may be interested in seeking to raise the tariff in that country could be regarded as provocative? I say that with the knowledge which we have before us at the present time, were we to do what hon. gentlemen opposite by their amendment apparently wish us to do, namely raise the tariff, we would' be creating in. the" minds of the American people the very sentiment which would cause them to raise their tariff higher perhaps than it was ever their intention to raise it. We do not intend to take any action of that provocative character-
Well, they have an explanation now, which perhaps will help to correct it.
I wish to repeat-and I do not think this can be made too clear-that so far as_ the United States tariff is concerned that is a matter which the government of that country must settle for itself in accordance with its own interest. And the United States will be the first to recognize, if in any action they take our trade with them is adversely affected, that it is our right and our duty, and should be and will be our policy to see to it that we make such arrangements with respect to our tariff as will further our interests in our own way.
Having said this much may I again make clear, what I wish above all else to make clear, not only in this connection but in all others, living as we do beside the United States as near neighbours, it is in the interests alike of the United States and of this country, and in the larger interests of^ the British Empire, that so far as we can, with respect to all our relations, we each conduct our affairs in a spirit which will help to advance mutual interest, and which will help to avoid steps that may lead in the opposite direction.
I lead the whole of that passage in order that it may not be said that I left out any part of it. Then there was a further question with respect to the matter of the British preference, which need not be mentioned now. I want to go a step further, however, because this affords me an opportunity of making this statement. We have to thank the action taken by this parliament in 1930 and the empire agreements for being able to make any contract at all with the United States. I say that, Mr. Speaker, not from hearsay; I have it direct from the government of the United States, that it was because we enacted the tariffs of 1930 and the agreements of 1932 that they were willing or desirous to negotiate with us at all, and that looks reasonable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Would my
right hon. friend produce the documents?

I said I had it from a
member of the government. Obviously I cannot mention names, for the reason the right hon. gentleman mentioned the other day, but he can verify that if he will make the'necessary application, and I will give him the name privately if he so desires.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think my right hon. friend should make mention of any statement unless he is able to give names.

What nonsense! I think the right hon. gentleman will agree that one may often have to make reference to what governments have said without referring to the person who made the statement. The government said it. And it is perfectly clear that but for the fact that Canada through this parliament in 1930 responded to the action of the United States by enacting the tariffs they did to protect this country fittingly against the adverse barriers that were raised against us, and enacted the British trade agreements, we should have had no proposals for any kind of reciprocity agreement at all. That I think is beyond question.
Let us go a step further. There continued until the end during the period of time that we were in office a constant endeavour to negotiate an agreement-I say, a constant endeavour. But during the election campaign I said on every platform what I repeat here, that I would not become a party to making any agreement with any country, not even the motherland, that gave anyone a preference over Canadians in the Canadian market. That is the position I took and always will take with respect to this country; and when I point out what the effect of this agreement is upon Canada and Canadian trade the house will understand why the government of that day was not prepared to enter into the agreement that has been entered into by hon. gentlemen opposite. We could have made an agreement such as is now before the house-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Why didn't
you?

The right hon. gentleman says, "Why didn't you?" Because I prefer my country to office and power. I can understand, sir, the smiles of some, the laughs and jeers of others, because before I conclude this statement I shall show that it is upon the very principles I enunciated that we oppose this agreement. We oppose it because it sacrifices Canada, because it is detrimental to the interests of this dominion, because it gives everything we have to give and gets little in return. That is why we object to it. That is why in 1899 Sir Wilfrid Laurier made the statement he did.
I said the other day that I would, and I am sorry I hurried on without doing it, give the American record of these proceedings. I now quote from what Mr. Foster said as to the attitude, not of this government but of the government led by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in days past with respect to these matters. He
Canada-U\S. Trade Agreement

realized how difficult it was to make a bargain; he realized what the effect of it would be, and he declined in 1898 to enter into an agreement. I shall read from what Mr. Foster said as to the circumstances under which he took that action. In his Diplomatic Memoirs, at the beginning of volume II, General Foster, who became Secretary of State of the United States, said:
I have referred in previous chapters to the interest manifested by President Arthur in the development of commercial reciprocity, and to the steps taken by his administration to inaugurate and carry forward such a system 9f exchange with foreign countries. His defeat in the national convention of his party in 1884, followed by the election of President Cleveland, who was opposed' to the system, resulted in the failure of the three treaties which had been negotiated with Mexico, with Spain for Cuba and Porto Rico, and with San Domingo.
. But the return of the Republicans to power m the election of President Harrison in 1888 revived the reciprocity projects. Special arrangements or treaties for the favoured exchange of products with other nations were not an entirely new measure. During the presidency of Jackson a treaty made with France (1831) contained commercial reciprocity provisions. In 1843 President Tyler instructed our minister to Prussia, Mr. Wheaton, to negotiate with the Germanic Customs Union, or Zollverin, "a commercial treaty, which, while it will open new advantages to the agricultural interests of the United States and a more free and expanded' field for commercial operations, will affect injuriously no existing interest in the union."
Then follows a statement of other measures, until he arrives at the time when in 1892 there was passed a tariff act containing provisions for reciprocity only one of which could in any circumstances have reference to Canada. He points out the difficulty of negotiating that, how in fact he did negotiate with the West Indies; Jamaica was the last to come in, and finally representatives of the Leeward Islands and others arrived in Washington to make treaties. There was difficulty with Jamaica until the very end. He proceeds to point out the difficulty they had with Germany, and then comes this significant statement, that the Liberal party had come into office in Canada and desired to negotiate an agreement. The Conservatives had sent down delegates three in number in 1892, and letters were received from various men in Canada who were friends of General Foster, pointing out that this was being used for political reasons, and that he should not negotiate with those Conservatives, although he must do his duty. Then Goldwin Smith went to Washington, and his letter is set out in this volume. Then this follows:
Since the reciprocity conference at Washington in 1892, the Liberal party had been

Quite active in Canadian politics, and had finally succeeded in driving the Conservatives from power. The Liberals have encouraged expectations that, once in control of the government, they would pursue a more enlightened and neighbourly policy towards the United States, but these expectations were doomed to disappointment. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, now Prime Minister, and Sir Louis Davies, another member of the new Liberal cabinet, accompanied the Canadian experts to Washington, and they and I attended the meeting of the experts.
After the labours of the latter had been concluded, I held several unofficial conferences with Messrs. Laurier and Davies, and sought to bring them to some agreement for the better protection of the seals; but they were unwilling to take up this subject alone, and insisted that we should enter upon a consideration of various other matters, prominent among which was the old question of commercial reciprocity.
Then he refers to the appointment of the joint high commission. The members on the part of the United States were Senators Fairbanks and Gray, Congressmen Dingley, John W. Foster, John A. Kasson, and T. J. Cool-idge; and on the part of Great Britain Lord Hersehell, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Richard Cartwright, Sir Louis H. Davies, and Hon. John Charlton, M.P., and on the part of Newfoundland, Sir James Winter.
After referring to the various meetings, and the failure of the commission, and having already placed on record the statement of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1899 as to what he felt about the failure, I quote these words from page 188:
It would be tedious if I should attempt to give even a brief resume of the weeks and months of laborious examination and discussion of the various subjects submitted to the commission. On several of them a practical agreement was reached. On the sealing question the general principle of settlement was agreed to, and doubtless the details could have been arranged. On reciprocity little progress was made. Notwithstanding the professions of the Liberals when out of power and in the heat of a political campaign, in the commission they assumed much the same position as the Conservative delegates who came to Washington in 1892.
Then he went on:
.... The commission adjourned at Washington February 20, 1899, never again to be reassembled.
What was the reason Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his associates in 1898 took the view they did? It is a matter of record; it was because they were asked to give too much for what they could secure in return. And when we come to this bargain that has been made by the right hon. gentleman I shall point out that had the principles which governed Sir

Having placed this upon Hansard, as I should have done a few minutes before, I desire to continue with respect to the negotiations. The right hon. gentleman has stated the conditions under which he entered into the negotiations; the limited powers of the president, the power to grant not more than fifty per cent reduction in the tariffs of the United States; the limitation as to time. And by the way, in that particular the right hon. gentleman did me an injustice. My objection in 1911 was to the fact that there was no time specified, but that it could be, as Mr. Fielding points out in his letter, terminated at the sweet will of either party without notice. But this agreement is for three years certain, a fixed period. It may be continued, and can be terminated only on six months' notice. I omitted to read one item from General Foster with respect to that; Germany raised the same question in dealing with her problems. She entered into an agreement with the United States and found it so unsatisfactory that she complained bitterly because when a new government came into office the agreement that had been made under a previous administration was no longer in force. And he says:
The most pronounced of these protests came from Germany while the bill was pending, in which the minister in Washington stated that the German agricultural and manufacturing circles entertained the belief above mentioned.
That is, that this was an unfair thing to do, to terminate the agreement they made. General Foster adds this very pregnant observation:
One of the inconveniences of our Republican form of government, with its recurring elections, is that it brings about sudden and radical changes of administration, so that it is difficult to maintain a uniform or permanent foreign commercial policy.
And then he refers to difficulties in connection with the senate approving any act of that kind. Hence it was that we asked that at least some period of time should be specified, because, by reason of circumstances to which I have referred, I have seen many men in western Canada engaged in the cattle business who have been ruined, as I said the other day, because they had no time to change their arrangements with respect to their herds before the provisions of the Underwood bill were ended.
One step further. Not only did Germany apply, but other countries did as well. This is one of the reasons why at one time we
considered ten years when negotiating the British-Canadian agreement. It was thought three years would be a fairer time, and three years was the term provided by the act of congress, commonly known as the trade agreements act. But congress was not prepared to grant to the president power by executive action beyond the period of three years, and then subject to the conditions I have mentioned. Further, they were insistent that the agreements should not last longer than three years, and if they did they should be subject to termination upon six months' notice.
I mention this because it becomes important to remember, in the light of what later transpired. And may I here point out this: It was said the other day by the right hon. gentleman opposite that until his death Sir Wilfrid Laurier kept on urging that there should be an acceptance of what might be called the standing offer by the government of the United States. Surely my right hon. friend has not forgotten that the Underwood tariff was passed in 1913, and that under that tariff we enjoyed free entry to the United States on practically all items that we were receiving free entry on under the reciprocity agreement, and we got this without giving anything, except one thing. We passed an order in council saying that wheat, wheat flour and semolina should have free entry into Canada because the United States had said that those three articles should freely enter their country to enable similar articles from their country to enter Canadian markets. Does anyone suggest-and I am sure my right hon. friend is not fair to his great leader -that the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was advocating that we should accept an agreement that was not as favourable to Canada as was the Underwood tariff? Does anyone suggest that? And Sir Wilfrid Laurier died in 1919, the Underwood tariff continuing until 1921, when the emergency tariff was passed in the United States. So that from 1913 to 1921 we had the Underwood tariff, with free access to the United States market for our cattle, for our fish, for our lumber, but with certain limitations with respect to certain kinds of lumber. The fact is, however, that we had access to the United States market on terms and conditions much more favourable than under the Taft-Fielding agreement, with respect to lumber, one of the great items of trade. The same may be said with respect to other items.
I do not desire to do more than direct the attention of the members of the house to the provisions of the Underwood tariff, because
Canada-UJ3. Trade Agreement

it is one of the most important of the many tariffs which have been passed in the United States. It represented in action the views of President Wilson, when he was a candidate. The Underwood tariff gave our cattle, our meat, our lumber and our fish, about which the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) used to speak, access to the markets of the United States.
But in 1921, when the new Republican party returned to office they enacted an emergency tariff which at once placed duties against many of these articles. As I said the other day, the cattle industry, for instance, is one which can flourish only if preparations are made for a term of years. You cannot market cattle with any degree of success under a short agreement; it takes one, two, three or perhaps four years to secure the best results. Out in western Canada when the emergency tariff was passed by the Republican congress of the United States, nullifying and destroying the Underwood tariff, it brought disaster and ruin to the larger cattle dealers of this country, a disaster from which they never recovered.
I think if hon. members will pause for a moment and consider they will realize that without paying anything in exchange, in 1913 President Wilson gave to Canada largely all, and in some instances more advantages than were obtained under the Taft-Fielding agreement of 1911, and that was only two years later. This indicates the uncertainty to which General Foster refers in connection with matters of this kind.
Here there was a country offering to do something for us. As Mr. Fielding said in the debate, we could not change a single item without voiding the whole. Sir Robert Borden asked him if it was indivisible, and he replied, "Yes, on all things." I will give one item, Portland cement, which carried eleven cents in the Fielding-Knox tariff agreement. The present rate is eight cents. It was reduced, and to reduce it would have meant an abrogation of the agreement. The same applies with respect to lumber; we received more favourable treatment with respect to lumber under the Underwood tariff than we did under the Fielding-Knox proposals. So that we have Sir Wilfrid Laurier making suggestions unsuccessfully, immediately after the reductions under the measure of 1911, that it should be availed of. But I have not been able to find any time after 1913, when the Underwood tariff came into being, that Sir Wilfrid Laurier suggested, publicly at least, that we should go back to a higher tariff structure for the purpose of enabling Canadians to trade. Of course there were in the Fielding-Knox agreement items that were

lower in tariff incidence than were the items in the Underwood tariff. But in the important items which affected us, cattle, fish and lumber, such was not the case. I mention that in passing.
Let us see what the real situation was that confronted the late government when they reached a point at which they had to decide whether they would or would not make an agreement on the proposals submitted. First, the Prime Minister has correctly stated the limitations upon the powers of the president. Those limitations were of such a character that if we got everything that he could give us we would get concessions of only fifty per cent on the tariff charges then made against us. I shall presently point out that if we got fifty per cent on every item in the tariff we would still be paying, in some instances, a higher tariff than that which prevailed under the Fordney-MeCumber rates. That is a fact to keep in mind. I shall give one illustration of this as I proceed. This is the position as I saw it, as my colleagues saw it, as the government saw it and as they instructed their minister to see it: First, the Dominion of Canada is a country with a population of less than eleven million people, inhabiting half a continent in the north temperate zone; on the other hand we find one hundred and twenty-seven million people who are inhabitants of a country with practically every variety of climate known to man. On the one hand, there was a new country without accumulated wealth undertaking a great development, a country that had built railroads on a great scale and that must look to increasing traffic if they were to maintain their economic position among the great nations of the world. On the other hand, there was a vast country, the richest in the world, a country of great reserve power represented by the accumulation of wealth. I shall not take time to refer to those conditions described by Mr. Blake or Sir Richard Cartwright as long ago as 1879, but here we were, a hardy, sturdy people, endeavouring to build a nation on the northern half of this continent, in the north temperate zone alongside a country of 127,000,000 of people inhabiting half a continent and with every variety of product being produced and every variety of climate that the world knows. Ah, more; for we were buying from them $28.86 worth per head during the year before while they were buying from us $2.23 per head.
That means nothing- multiply it by ten.

It may not mean anything to hon. gentlemen opposite but it means a great deal to those who think seriously, and

I will tell you why. The net result was that it made an unfavourable balance of trade against this country of hundreds of millions of dollars, and that is an important thing to keep in mind.
I will go a step further and give the figures for 1934 with respect to trade balances, because I regard them as being of the utmost importance. What was our position? We have a commodity balance, which is a visible balance, and we have an invisible balance of interest, insurance and freights; and these together constitute the relations of one country to the other with respect to trade. In 1934, according to an estimate made by United States authorities, and which agree in the main with the figures supplied by our own bureau of statistics, the United States had a 370,000,000 credit on the commodity exchange between the two countries; and mark you, in 1934 it had been reduced to $70,000,000 by the most painful efforts that a government ever had to undertake. We either had to reduce that $200,000,000 which it once was to a lower figure or else we had to default; there was no question as to that. That was the position with which we were faced.
On our tourist traffic we had a favourable balance in 1934 of $74,000,000; in other words, this tourist industry in 1934 overcame the adverse commodity or trading balance against this country and there was an excess of $4,000,000 in our favour. We had reduced, on the one hand, the trading balance against us by every means within our power, and on the other hand we had stimulated the development of tourist traffic by every means at our disposal.
On immigration, remittances and charities, once more the balance was against us to the amount of $3,000,000.
Then, we come to shipping and freight: On freight passing through the United States and coming into this country they had a claim against us of $6,000,000. On miscellaneous items they had a further charge against us of $6,000,000. On total goods and services there was another balance of $5,000,000 in favour of the United States.
With respect to interest payments in 1934 they amounted to $51,000,000 against us. When I come to direct earnings on investments, that is, the income received by Canadians as against the income paid to people in the United States by people in Canada, there was a balance in favour of the United States of $48,000,000. Bank transactions in their favour amounted to $4,000,000.
Then we did what we have not been accustomed to do in years gone by. By reason of the action taken by this parliament, gold was no longer being treated for purely monetary purposes, and so we treated our exports of gold to the United States as a commodity, and that gave us a favourable balance against the United States of $87,000,000. Then the silver balance and the currency balance was against us to the amount of $2,000,000. So that at the end of 1934, despite the most heroic struggles from 1930 to 1934 that a people have ever made to meet the situation that had developed by reason of the circumstances to which I have referred, the United States had a balance against this dominion of $19,000,000.
We pointed out in the note that we sent to them that this disparity should be dealt with in some way, and we had a right to ask them not only to treat us on an equality basis, but if they desired to give us an opportunity for fair treatment, shall I say, we should have the maximum benefits that could come to us under the limited powers which the president possessed. Confronted with that adverse balance which we had to meet there were other matters which we had to think of. Let us see what they were. Let us look them fairly in the eye.
When we were negotiating for an agreement we were not ignorant of the fact that the exports of this country, exclusive of our domestic requirements, were a matter of transcendent importance not only to our monetary system but with respect to our whole economic structure and life. It may not generally be known, but the fact is that the population of Canada has shifted to the extent that one half of our people are now living in cities and towns. That happened for the first time at the time of the census of 1931, and the trend has increased since. There are more and more people now in cities and towns looking for employment in factories, mills and industrial plants of various kinds than ever before. According to the bureau of statistics, in the year 1934, 82%o per cent in value of all our agricultural production was used at home, and only 17ts per cent of our entire agricultural production found a market abroad. That includes everything. Let us go a step further; let us look at manufactures.

I am one of those who have always been more or less alarmed and concerned about the favoured nation clauses in our treaties. I confess I found it difficult to negotiate with France when by our granting a concession to France on a suggested item some other country would get the benefit of it and France would not get it at all. That was true of many items that were discussed in connection with the French treaty, and the French withdrew from their position when they saw that not they but somebody else would profit by it.
