But I put this to the house; the other day I picked up the Congressional Record and I read a speech in which a member for Carolina pointed out that this was going to be a great thing for him; his furniture sales had been seriously cut down, but now he would be able to recover his lost market I want to know. There is a large number of items on which it is clearly apparent that unless some action is taken the result from this agreement will be greatly to decrease employment in Canada. That is clear. But in addition to that it is common ground that very substantial injury will be done to those who have invested their capital in this country. I am not here to argue for a single moment that every vested interest in this country has a right to perpetual-
Pap.

Well, let hon. gentlemen laugh, but my reading of the history of my country is that we have built up employment for one half of our population by the application of a protective tariff:	You can call it
pap if you like; all I can say is that successive governments have done it. The government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not behind others in doing it; and having done it, with our eyes open we have created these industries. I have said before in this house that there are some industries in this country that I would never have created, but they are here; they will be here long after I am gone, and the question now is whether they are entitled to fair consideration and fair play. We said we would leave that to the tariff board, and I find that this agreement proposes to leave some factors and some difficult problems to be determined- by the tariff board. The former Minister of Finance gave effect to every finding and recommendation made by the tariff board that he received in time to give effect to while he held office, every one of them. It would be presumption for me to express any view with respect to the question of sufficiency or insufficiency of tariff protection, but by taking the action this agreement contemplates, injuries will inevitably result. There is one way to cure them, and that is in many instances to increase the intermediate tariff. I think I am within my rights, as every hon. member of this house is within his rights, in saying that before I stand in my place and vote on this agreement I want to know whether there is to be at this session an increase in the intermediate tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There might be decreases also.

There may be decreases; one is not arguing that there may not. The government may reduce every item in the tariff except those with respect to which they are bound to specific duties or free entry, those they cannot alter, either under the United States agreement or any other agreement where similar conditions prevail. But the question is, is there to be any increase in the intermediate tariff? I leave it to any fairminded man in this house whether he does not think he has a right to know whether or not that intermediate tariff structure is to be changed at this session, before he votes to give effect to this resolution. For if it is changed, the resolution he votes on and that which will be in force will not be the same. The bill founded on it will not be the same. If the tariff bill is passed later of course it will modify pro tanto the provisions of the trade agreement we are now considering.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not of the agreement.
Of course it will.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The agreement specifically reserves to this parliament the right to change.
Yes, that is what I say, and if there is a modification of the rates that now prevail, the agreement that we enact and the agreement which will be in force will not be the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all.
Well, put it this way, in order that there may be no haggling; the situation will not be the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The effect will not be
precisely the same.

Canada-VJS. Trade Agreement

Certainly the effect will
not be precisely the same; that is all I want. And since it will not be precisely the same, has not this house the right to know whether or not there will be a change in the intermediate tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then equally the house
has a right to know what the government is going to propose next year or the year after that with respect to the intermediate tariff.

No; in a given session
we can deal only with sessional matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And. we cannot deal
with the budget until it is down.

I agree, but I say any
change that might be made with respect to the intermediate tariff affecting this agreement would not be fair to the house unless the house knows before the agreement is adopted, what the changes are to be. It is simply a matter of fair play.
Now I will give a list of items that I think must be considered by this government. Item 16, eggs: existing general tariff, ten cents; intermediate, five cents. Oats, sixteen cents; down to nine cents. When the item is before the committee I wonder what explanation the government is going to give for wild oats not fit for human consumption getting the reduced rates while oats fit for human consumption are not dealt with. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) should at least make a protest over that. Take wheat, another item that must be considered: it carries to-day thirty cents against the United States; under the intermediate it is twelve cents. Wheat flour, $1.35; intermediate, fifty cents. I can recall in my younger days when the flour went to the maritime provinces, as the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) can tell you, came from Boston in schooners at practically no freight rate at all; it could easily pay fifty cents a barrel duty.	Is that to remain?	That
is a question for consideration. Then, hay: at the present time the rate on hay is $5; under the new tariff it is $1.75. Is that to remain, or not? Under the old tariff the duty on potatoes was seventy-five cents; the new rate is free. Is that to continue? Is Maine to supply potatoes to upper Canada? Is Michigan to supply Windsor her requirements free of duty, or are Canadians to do this? This has to be considered. Then, onions, thirty per cent, with a specific duty, as against thirty per cent. Mushrooms and truffles thirty per cent with a specific duty as against twenty-seven and a half per cent. On fresh fruits the duty is reduced to fifteen per cent.
Yes.

My hon. friend approves that. But remember this: There can be destruction of no industry, however small it may be, without injury to the whole economic structure of our country.
Then, let us take advertising. Advertising, when less than twenty per cent, paid two cents a copy. These items are now free. This advertising, I believe, is one of the most insidious of the, shall I say, unseen influences which have to do with the formation of national character. I think it will be found that that is so. That position is true of wall board, wall paper and paper containers, rods, bars, and sheets and plates of brass. Parts of watch movements are reduced to five cents specific duty, instead of ten cents. Then, farm implements are mentioned, in which we are carrying on a large export trade which cannot possibly be maintained, unless the former duty is restored. Then, there are washing machines, machinery, nuts and bolts, middle range automobiles and trucks, manufactures of steel, furniture, linoleum and oil cloth, and several other commodities I might mention, without going into them at length.
I put this question, and ask it very seriously: Are we to be told before we vote upon this agreement whether it is a real one that is to be effective, or whether the intermediate tariff is to be raised so that these various industries and agriculture products which are matters of concern, shall be cared for? Let us ask ourselves one more question with respect to this matter, and it is this: What is the effect of this agreement upon agriculture and agricultural products, including dairy products? Let us answer that. The duty on cream is reduced so that it occupies a position equivalent to eight cents a pound on butter. The old Fordney-McCumber tariff was twenty cents; this is now thirty-five cents, with a quota. I shall refer to this point presently. Name me any agricultural products which benefit by this agreement. Name any agricultural product which in the ultimate analysis benefits by this agreement. Let us take dairy products on the farm. We will pass live stock; as regards live stock undoubtedly there is a benefit, but that is not a fifty per cent benefit-and that is the odd part of the matter -as we shall point out in committee. If we are dealing with these items why could we not get at least a fifty per cent reduction with respect to cattle, and commodities of that nature? Is it worth while entering into an agreement merely for the sake of saying, "We have signed an agreement inside of ninety days; we had been in office only a few days, and see what we did"? Is that for the

Canada-UJS. Trade Agreement
economic welfare of Canada? That is the real issue which must be considered.
Then, turning again to the tariff we find we have now a quota on lumber. Who introduced quotas? Tell me this: Is there a single quota which Canada has imposed against the United States? If there is, name it. But look at the list of quotas imposed against us. Why should quotas be imposed against us when we did not get even fifty per cent? Let us take fish. What do we get for fish? Look at the Underwood tariff; look at the free fish. Shall it be said that, because of the depressed condition in Gloucester and surrounding - territory, where they have trawlers which go out on the open sea and the grand banks, Canadians, without trawlers, endeavouring to compete in United States ports are denied that privilege to the extent of .fifty per cent of existing duties. There is a depression here, too, in the fishing industry. The farm, the forest, the sea, the mine-what have we as regards the mines? We have a few articles that have relation to hydro electric power, as was pointed out; and even as to them, what is their relation to the whole? I am asking that question seriously. What are they? Study them, and answer me. What answer can be given?
There is, it is true, a reduction in the duty on liquor, on cattle and on whiskey. There was never any question about the duty on whiskey, because whiskey in the United States has not matured. If we get rid of our whiskey before the date of maturity of theirs we shall have succeeded in benefiting from this agreement. Otherwise, we shall not. We must dispose of our whiskey during the period the United States whiskey is maturing.
What about our parts manufacturers in Canada? I am not going to do more than point out that we have afforded them protection. The assembly plants of this country have utilized the parts produced in Canadian mills and factories, and have utilized them to an enormous extent. I have knowledge of the fact that there have been cancellations of orders for these items. Are we going to pass an intermediate tariff which will give greater protection to these items? These are questions which will have to be dealt with.
What has been done with respect to any of these commodities? For instance, we have bran, shorts and wheat-what about them? Are they free? No. Is the duty reduced to any extent at all? No. It is fixed at ten per cent, where it stood the day before the agreement was signed. Look at the items. Then there are hulled oats, unfit for human consumption, with a duty of eight cents per
bushel of thirty-two pounds. There is nothing for oatmeal. Then there is wheat, unfit for human consumption, with a duty of ten per cent ad valorem, the rate at which it stood before. Not a cent of reduction in duty for entry of wheat into the United States of America, although we have reduced our duty on their wheat to the extent I have indicated. On bran, shorts, byproduct feeds obtained in milling wheat or other cereals, the rate is ten per cent ad valorem. On mixed feeds it is ten .per cent ad valorem, and on screenings, ten per cent, the same old rate. On cereal breakfast foods, we have in this instance a reduction in duty from twenty per cent ad valorem to fifteen per cent, or a decrease of five per cent. When we come to grass seeds we find a fifty per cent reduction. My point is this: Why did we not hold out for a fifty per cent reduction with respect to all these items if we were going to get a fifty per cent reduction on this or that? Had we not a right to ask for this?
Then there are large numbers of items to which I shall give no more than hasty consideration. First, we have oats and barley. How will the change in ths rate on barley affect Prince Edward Island? What about the pelts of silver foxes which come from the island? The silver fox industry is one of the greatest down there, but we find a fifty per cent ad valorem duty on these pelts entering the United States-no reduction. On certain pelts, however, the rate was reduced. On wolves' pelts-and I can understand this-the duty was reduced. But on pelts of silver foxes, an item which touches vitally the economic life of the island, there was no reduction; the fifty per cent rate still remains.
Then we come to other items, a number of which I have mentioned. Did we get a fifty per cent out on cattle? We did not. We secured a reduction, but it was not fifty per cent, the maximum, which we should have received. We did get something else; we got a quota on them. I put to the house just one question with respect to this situation: Looking at those schedules can it be said that we have received adequate consideration for what we have given? That is the question. The right hon. gentleman put it yesterday fairly. That is the issue. Well, sir, I put this to you and to the house: Does it ever occur to hon. members that during an election any prime minister would be anxious to sign a trade agreement because of the effect which this might have upon the mind of the electorate? If he did not sign it; if the government could not approve proposals that did

Canada-UJS. Trade Agreement
not give to the Dominion of Canada concessions that were adequate to those which we gave, only one thing can be said, that the temptation to sign any agreement is very strong, and the fact that it was not signed is at least some indication that there was strong conviction that it was not adequate. There is the story.
The right hon. gentleman said something about the future. I put this to him:	What
more can we give the United States than we have already given them under this agreement? What have we left to negotiate with? There is the position; there is the situation, and I can only say that the government of the day was not prepared to grant the concessions contained in this agreement for what we consider the wholly inadequate advantages accruing under it to the Dominion of Canada, notwithstanding the effect that it might have upon the minds of the electorate.
The right hon. gentleman was right the other day in saying that it was in September that the note was given to the public. The government of the United States did not think it desirable that during negotiations there should be any publication of the note, and so we did not publish it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My right hon. friend was mistaken about having tabled it.

The hon. gentleman was right it was not tabled in the house. Twice I had the note ready to table, and twice I was advised by the minister that it was undesirable to do so. I was in error in thinking that it had been tabled, and I desire to make that perfectly clear.
Contemporary opinion in one country is not always a guide to the action of another country. Of course, most members of the house have seen the article that appeared in the Independent Journal of Columbia University written by Professor Brebner, in which he speaks of Canada's tariff gamble and says that this is an excellent treaty for defying economic nationalism. He says that Canada has made more concessions increasing her economic vulnerability. I am not going to take time to do more than point out his conclusion, that this would be injurious to Canada. Without going into the matter, I may say that he points out our vulnerability and says in effect'that this is a huge gamble; that if it succeeds it is a good thing, and if it does not, it is a very bad thing for the future of this dominion.
I cannot think, Mr. Speaker, that we are warranted in gambling about such a serious

matter, and when I look at the observations made by the President of the United States himself and by his Secretary of Agriculture, Mr. Wallace, I realize that they refer to this agreement as affording a market in the Dominion of Canada for their manufactured products as well as their agricultural products. These words were used by the Secretary of State, Mr. Cordell Hull, in a letter to Mr. Costigan:	He said that the restrictions with
respect to cattle will "assure the most ample protection to our domestic cattle producers." He continues:
The small concession which we have granted on cattle must be considered, if its real significance is to be appreciated, in the broad light of the entire agreement ... and of the benefits which will derive of this agreement in the shape of hundreds of millions of dollars in increased' exports, a large part of which will largely consist of agricultural exports, while the remainder of the increase will be in industrial products, which, through enlarged payrolls and augmented purchasing power will inevitably rebound to the ultimate benefit of our cattle raising and farming sections.
Mr. Henry A. Wallace, the very able Secretary of Agriculture, speaking at Chicago on December 10, said that it was his considered judgment that American agriculture gains from the Canadian reciprocal trade treaty "so far outweigh the losses that the net advantage to our agriculture as a whole is very much worth while." He said that Canadian concessions on meats and meat products duties will open the way "for our farmers to get back a bigger share of the British pork market. The new agreement will permit American pork to go to Canada to replace Canadian pork exported to Great Britain, thus, in effect permitting increased exports of American pork to Great Britain." He claimed important benefits to fruit and vegetable growers through Canadian concessions and said that those benefits would be "substantial gains" for United States grain growers. "Farmers of the United States will unquestionably gain from the increased exportation of manufactured products to Canada," he said. He went on:
Suppose that exports of these products are increased by $300,000,000-a conservative figure in view of our trade with Canada in the past -and that half of this amount or $150,000,000 goes into payrolls.
This would mean definite and substantial gains in cash income of farmers. Studies have shown that in the past an increase of $150,000,000 in United States factory payrolls added from four to six million dollars to the income of farmers in each of such states as Illinois, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Nebraska, Missouri, Iowa and Ohio.

Canada-UJi. Trade Agreement
The President himself said:
Agriculture, far from being crucified by this agreement, as some have told you, actually gains from it. We export more agricultural products to Canada than we have imported from her. We shall continue to do so, for the very simple reason that the United States with its larger area of agricultural land, its more varied climate and its vastly greater population produces far more of mpst agricultural products, including animal products, vegetables and fruits, than does Canada. In the case of the few reductions that have been made, quota limitations are set on the amount that may be brought in at the lower rates.
On the other side of the picture we believe, and most unbiased men believe, that the general increase in our trade with Canada, including the exports of our factories, will so add to the purchasing power of hundreds of thousands of wage earners that they will be able to spend far more than they do to-day for the products of our own farms, our own forests and our own fisheries. Greater trade is merely another word for more production and more employment. The proof of this particular pudding is in the eating; the best way to judge the new accord is to observe how it works out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Has my right
hon. friend any observations by ex-President Hoover?
He did not have anything to do with this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He had a lot to say.

I am only going to
follow up what I have read by saying this: Varying views will be entertained with respect to the benefits and disadvantages of this agreement. There are those who will argue that the benefits far outweigh the disadvantages. There are Canadians who will argue, as they have done, that the benefits greatly exceed the disadvantages. On the other hand, there will be Canadians who see in this agreement, as I do, not only a balance of disadvantages against benefits but an act on the part of the government that can only-can only, I repeat-result in great injury to Canada unless we avail ourselves of the provisions of the intermediate tariff and at this session increase it with respect to many items to which I have referred. That, I think, is inevitable. On the other hand, in the United States there are those who say that the bargain is bad for the United States, and there are those who say it is highly advantageous; one is a supporter of the administration and the other is opposed to it. But that is not so everywhere. There are men who left office because they felt that the agreement was not satisfactory from the standpoint of the United States. There are Canadians who view it with alarm, and there are Canadians who rejoice at it.
I can only say that each of us must arrive at his own conclusion in the light of the knowledge he possesses of the fundamental economic position of this country. This agreement is predicated upon the assumption that there will be a great increase in purchasing power in Canada within the next few years. I am not one of those who do not believe that we shall gradually improve our condition, but when I heard the right hon. gentleman the other day take 1929 as a basis for comparison, I wondered why he took that year. For in 1929 the Fordney-McCumber tariff was in force and that tariff imposed, against Canadian trade, barriers never before known until the Hawley-Smoot tariff of 1930. That is a fact which the ordinary figures indicate; they show the trade of this country before and after the enactment of that measure. I can only say that we are placed in a very difficult position. In good faith, desiring to extend Canadian trade in accordance with the traditions of our party, we made as a basis for negotiation proposals that were broad and generous, giving an opportunity to consider every item in the tariff structure of both countries.

My right hon. friend has
said that the minimum demand we should have made upon the United States was for a straight fifty per cent reduction in their tariff against us all along the line. I should like to know whether he made that demand and whether the reason why no agreement was reached under his administration was the fact that the United States refused to make that concession.	*

That question is simply
answered. Mr. Hull, the Secretary of State, as the communications read by the right hon. gentleman the other day show, said that each item would have to be considered. Proposals and counter-proposals were made, and when these proposals, which are now practically the proposals of the United States, were presented to us we said definitely that we could not give them such concessions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They are not practically the same.

The right hon. gentleman says that they are not practically the same. It is true that with respect to cattle we had a fifty per cent cut with a limitation on values; this is less than a fifty per cent cut with a quota as to numbers. This, I think, should be a fair answer: The government of the day was not prepared to grant the concessions asked for in return for the concessions which the United States expressed themselves willing to grant.

Canada-UjS. Trade Agreement

I am afraid the leader of
the opposition missed the point of my question. I was not particularly referring to the concessions we were giving to the United States; I was asking about the concessions which were demanded by Canada from the United States. Was the demand made that there should be a straight fifty per cent reduction all along the line so far as the United States tariffs were concerned?

There were two discussions, one as to an agreement of a limited kind, the other being an agreement in the large sense now before us. And before we could get any further in the matter the demands were such that we said that anything granted would not be adequate compensation for what was asked, not even fifty per cent.

Did you ask for fifty per
cent?

The question is not
whether we asked for fifty per cent; we said fifty per cent would not be adequate.

I understood the right hon.
gentleman to say that we should not have concluded any agreement unless we received at least a minimum of fifty per cent all along the line, and I am curious to know whether he asked for that concession and whether, it being refused, he did not conclude an agreement.

Let me answer that
question in this way:	I said that if my
hon. friends were going to come here with an agreement they should at least have taken as a minimum the maximum the United States would grant, which was fifty per cent of existing tariff rates. But I said that the concessions asked for were such that at no price were we prepared to grant them. I want to make that clear beyond peradven-ture. It is not a question of fifty per cent or any other percentage; we made it clear that neither fifty per cent nor sixty per cent would be adequate for the concessions asked from us, because it took away from us everything we had: the whole intermediate tariff, the favoured nation clause, the binding on the free list and the loss of direct shipment, so that for the first time in our history there might be a through bill of lading; it was no longer to river, lake or seaport but to inland customs port.
My question was definite.

And I have answered it
as definitely as it is possible to answer it. We could not and would not give to the

United States what this agreement gives, in return for anything which it was within the power of the president to grant. Is that clear?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Are we to
understand from the right hon. gentleman's remarks that negotiations were definitely terminated before he went out of office?

No. They were in this
position, that in October it became perfectly clear that we could not succeed in securing an agreement on the basis I have mentioned, the basis of this agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Not of this
agreement.
It was substantially what this agreement embodies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

I say that it embodies
what the United States asked us to give and we would not give.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My right hon. friend knows that negotiations of the kind are confidential; but when he makes the Statement that this agreement is one that he could have made and one that was offered to him at the time, he knows that is not the case.

Well, I repeat that the
proposals of the United States were substantially those embodied in the concessions which have been submitted to this house; I say that positively and without question. And what is more, we never did reach a draft agreement; a draft agreement was never prepared. But I will tell you more. Mr. Foster, in his memoirs, points out that during the progress of negotiations with the United States he received intimation that somebody else would do something better; and there is no doubt that during the negotiations, during the last two months that we were in office, there was circulated, throughout official circles in the United States, the idea that if the Liberals got in they would do better than we had done. That was circulated in season and out of season, stated on public platforms by the right hon. gentleman, that they could negotiate agreements where we could not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have.
Certainly; but agreements which we would not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Which you could not.

There is one thing I
deprecate. I greatly deprecate the attitude of the Prime Minister with respect to this and

Canada-UJS. Trade Agreement
all other matters. The other day he saved a war in Europe; to-day he has made an agreement at which all the world is sitting up and wondering. I think it ill becomes one occupying the position of Prime Minister to try to make the people believe that wars and rumours of war have been stilled and peace has been secured because he repudiated Mr. Riddell in Geneva, and that the world's economic peace, liberty and happiness depend upon his having made these concessions to the United States; that we got all that we could get, which is enough, because we have restored the balance in the world's economy and all is well in Israel. That, I say, is an attitude of mind which is not conducive to the well-being of the country. It is magnifying oneself to an extent which I think is not warranted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Don't speak
of magnifying oneself, please; please don't. Spare us that.

It makes us a bit
ridiculous in some quarters. It has been the subject matter of a good deal of ridicule in different places that these 11,000,000 people, having made a bargain with the United States, have saved the economic peace of the world, and that the repudiation of a representative of ours in Geneva by the then acting Prime Minister saved the world from war, if only the facts were known. That is not conducive to this country being held in that esteem in which it should be regarded among the nations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
You would describe it
in Mr. Thomas's terms.

The hon. gentleman, in
his solicitude for vested interests, may well speak in that way, but the fact is that he will find it more difficult to deal with the British agreements by reason of the agreement now before the house, much more difficult. Then the smile and jeer that he has for those who toiled with these agreements will probably give way to some sympathetic understanding of what they did for this country when they made them, and his anxiety to serve the interests that he so nobly serves will perhaps give way to a little consideration for the people of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What does my right hon. friend mean?
Just what he says.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What did he say?
I said that the interests he serves so nobly-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What are they?

They are the great interests of this country. Never have they been served better by any Minister of Finance than by the hon. gentleman, as everybody knows and as has come to be very generally understood.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The great interests of this country?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The interests of the people of this country?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not of the people?
The interests that have been discussed in the house. The so-called great interests. The St. James' street interests he used to speak about; the milling interests-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker: my hon. friend has just stated in effect that I represent in this house certain special interests; that I serve them here nobly. There is a word which the rules of the house will not allow me to apply to my hon. friend. He knows what it is, and he knows that it would be correctly applied. I demand that he withdraw unconditionally. The statement he has made is absolutely without foundation, and he well knows that.
Anything that I know, Mr. Speaker, is correctly indicated by what I said. If the hon. gentleman feels offended at what has been said-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, sir, not because I feel any offence but because it is contrary to the rules of the house, and is untrue.
The rules of the house are quite clear, and I have not transgressed them. If we look at the observations of the last five years from his side of the house-
That is not what we are talking about.

-we shall find that they were always in use and applied when they were attacking others. Now when an observation is made with respect to himself, my hon. friend becomes very hot and very much worried.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have never applied such observations to any hon. member, and my right hon. friend knows I have never applied them to him. He knows how unfair, unjust and untrue they are as applied to me. I insist on an unqualified withdrawal.
Will the right hon. the leader of the opposition, withdraw?
Mr. Speaker, I am bound to accept your ruling and withdraw the remark.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Thank you.
All I did was to direct attention to the fact that the records of Hansard are filled with similar observations applied to others, including myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not by me.

I admit that the hon.
gentleman is sui generis in his party. So far as his party is concerned, that has been their stock in trade.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is not
true.
Unquestionably.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

Never has any man in
Canada been vilified in this house and attacked in every part of Canada more than I; and the people are beginning to know this and understand it. I shall follow it up with some data-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With regard to me?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With regard to me?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All right; go on.

That is what I say and
it is exactly what I mean, Mr. Speaker. Let there be no misunderstanding about it.
In concluding my observations I would say that there are differences of opinion with regard to this agreement both in the United States and Canada. We have the right to know whether this is an agreement that represents the real determination of the government within the rights conferred upon them to modify the intermediate tariffs, and until such time as we receive that information we cannot, I submit, fairly or honestly vote upon this agreement. We are entitled to that information, and I ask that it be given to us or that the consideration of the items in the agreement be dealt with as items in the ways and means committee when the budget is being considered.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, having had to take up so much time in reading so many extracts in dealing with this subject, but no more important matter has ever engaged the attention of parliament, nor is any more

important matter likely to engage its attention, than the one now before us. If we ask for the fullest information in order that we may be able intelligently to discuss it I think we ask for what is our right. This is expected of us by the Canadian people, by our several constituents and by those in every part of the country affected by the agreement, and until such time as we know whether the intermediate tariff is to be modified, increased or reduced at this present session of parliament we cannot properly deal with the agreement or give effect to its schedules.

I am sure that the house will freely acknowledge its indebtedness to both the right hon. gentlemen who have participated in this debate. I should like at the outset to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), first upon the success that attended his efforts in negotiating this trade agreement and then upon the very complete and masterly presentation which he made of the case in favour of this resolution. May I likewise compliment the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) upon the interesting and forceful address which he has just delivered in the house. He has made perfectly clear to hon. members and to the people of Canada his opposition to this trade agreement as it stands, and I think he has also made it perfectly clear that if the Canadian people had elected a Conservative administration Canada would not now have any trade agreement with the United States. May I also add a personal tribute to the Prime Minister for the splendid thought that actuated him in endeavouring to conclude his negotiations with the United States so that he might be able to announce on November 11, Armistice Day, the making of an agreement between Canada and the United States, thereby, Mr. Speaker, setting an example to the rest of the world in that on Armistice Day Canada and the United States were thinking of trade in terms of peace when much of the rest of the world was thinking of war.
It will not be possible for me, in the short space of time at my disposal, to deal with the various items in the schedules attached to the trade agreement, but I should like to state certain fundamental principles and certarn reasons why I for one support this agreement We on this side of the house support it for a number of reasons. In the first place it shows a new attitude towards international trade. It recognizes officially that the Liberal party regards trade not as war but as the peaceful exchange of goods based upon mutual advantage. That was recognized by the persona

Canada-TJ&. Trade Agreement
who took part in the signing of the agreement Mr. Cordell Hull, Secretary of State of the United States, made this statement:
Underlying this agreement are the twin policies of the good neighbour and mutually profitable trade.
When the Prime Minister spoke the other day he made perfectly clear the attitude of the Liberal party. In the course of his remarks he said:
May I say at once that we sought an agreement which would be fair and square and which would be helpful to both countries.
I submit also, Mr. Speaker, that this agreement will provide freer entry into the United States of a great number of primary products than has been the case heretofore. We have had concessions given to us with regard to agricultural products, fishery products, forest products and mineral products. The right hon. leader of the opposition sought to minimize the extent of these concessions to the primary producers of Canada. In a sense perhaps we ought to feel grateful to him for his remarks, because they will strengthen the hands of President Roosevelt in repelling the attacks that are being made in the United States against this agreement, on the grounds that the United States will be flooded with Canadian products. That is the argument there; we have heard the contrary argument here. Somewhere between the two lies the truth, and the truth is that the agreement is based on fair and square dealing on the basis of mutual advantage. I for one rejoice at the reversal of the trend of policy of the United States. The president of the United States made reference to this change when he said:
The signing of this agreement marks the reversal of the trend of the last two decades towards undue and unnecessary trade barriers between our two countries. I am confident that this constructive step will contribute greatly to the economic recovery of both the United States and Canada.
The basic wealth of Canada is in its primary production, but that basic wealth is of no value to those who produce it unless it can be made to circulate. We' on this side of the house feel that this trade agreement will stimulate the circulation of that basic wealth, with benefit to the body politic.
There is another reason why we support this trade agreement. We feel that it will ease the burden of the primary producer. There are reductions in the duty on implements of production, and it is essential to the welfare of the primary producer that his costs of production should be lowered in every possible way. Indeed there are many
of us on this side who would criticize this trade agreement in that it does not go far enough in the reduction of duties.
This agreement also remembers one who was forgotten during the lifetime of the previous administration. I refer to the consumer; the tariff reductions now provided for will reduce the cost of living to the consumers of Canada.
During the course of this debate mention has been made of the Ottawa agreements. I express the hope that never again will this country make an agreement along the lines and principles of the Ottawa agreements. I regard them as a dangerous step in the direction of economic imperialism. They are based upon wrong principles of bargaining and they are restrictive of trade agreements with other countries of the world. The trade agreement with the United Kingdom contained a very dangerous and iniquitous clause; I refer to article 9, which reads:
His Majesty's government in Canada will invite parliament to pass the legislation necessary to substitute for the duties of customs now leviable on the goods specified in schedule E the duties shown in that schedule, provided that nothing in this article shall preclude His Majesty's government in Canada from reducing the duties specified in the said schedule so long as the margin of British preference shown in that schedule is preserved or from increasing the rates under the intermediate or general tariff set out in the said schedule.
I stress the words, "so long as the margin of British preference shown in that schedule is preserved," and I say that as long as that clause remains in the Ottawa agreements it is impossible, in respect of the articles covered by them, to make with other countries such trade treaties as we should like to make. As an illustration I mention cream separators. In 1930 cream separators entered this country free under all tariffs. Our importations for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1930, totalled $955,000, of which 71 [DOT] 4 per cent came from the United States, 13-6 per cent from Sweden, six per cent from Denmark, and 3-4 per cent from France, with no importations at all from Great Britain. Then both the intermediate and general tariffs were increased to twenty-five per cent while cream separators continued to come in free under the British preference. In 1935 the total importations fell to $362,788. Only 11-4 per cent of our importations of cream separators came from Great Britain, and a duty of twenty-five per cent was imposed on 88-6 per cent of our imports of cream separators. A monopoly was created in Canada in respect of these articles. Our hands are tied with regard to cream separators;
Canada-UJS. Trade Agreement

as long as the Ottawa agreements are in effect we cannot make a trade treaty affecting cream separators with any of the countries with which we trade. Further than that, we cannot reduce the duty on cream separators below twenty-five per cent as long as the Ottawa agreements remain in force, because we have guaranteed to the United Kingdom a twenty-five per cent margin of preference. This is an iniquitous clause, which should be repealed when the Ottawa agreements come up for revision.
There are fundamental and important differences between this agreement and the Ottawa agreements. In this agreement we are making a retreat from economic imperialism and breaking the crust of economic nationalism. Both economic imperialism and economic nationalism are wrong policies for this country to follow; the only safe course for Canada to travel in matters of trade is that of internationalism, and we are now travelling on that safe highway in the direction of greater world trade, while the right hon. leader of the opposition and his followers are still mired in the slough of economic nationalism. No country is more dependent upon foreign markets than is Canada; no country is more dependent upon export trade, even though the percentage of our total production that is exported is as the leader of the opposition stated this afternoon. Export trade and foreign markets are of prime importance to the Dominion of Canada.
There is another reason why this trade agreement is preferable to the Ottawa agreements; the latter were restrictive of trade, and they have had the effect of creating an unfriendly sentiment in Great Britain towards Canada. There was a sigh of relief in Great Britain when the previous administration was so overwhelmingly defeated at the polls, just as there was a sigh of relief in this country. On the other hand the United States trade agreement will be productive of trade arrangements with other countries. This country will receive the benefit of all such trade treaties as the United States will make with other countries, and the benefits of all such treaties will inure to Canada. There is no guarantee of any fixed margin of preference in this agreement, and there is nothing to prevent reductions of duties. If I had been asked the question whether we are going to increase the intermediate tariff my answer would have been emphatically in the negative.
Another reason why we favour this trade agreement in preference to the Ottawa agreements is that in this one all the revisions of

tariff duties are downward, which was not so in the case of the Ottawa agreements. I am one of those who feel that, when the time comes to consider what shall be done with regard to the Ottawa agreements, there should be a drastic revision of them.
The Liberal party was returned to power by a tremendous majority. The voice of the people spoke with no uncertain sound. That voice expressed discontent with existing conditions and with the policy of the previous administration. If there was any mandate at all in that vote of the Canadian people it was most emphatically a mandate that there should be substantial tariff reductions.
I should like to compliment the Prime Minister upon the campaign that he conducted during the last election. He appealed for the suffrages of the people on fundamental principles and refused to be led into any campaign of competitive promises. The Liberal tariff policy has been clearly laid down. It was laid down in Winnipeg on January 12, 1932, when the Prime Minister stated:
As time goes on conditions change, and what for yesterday may have been the wisest step, for to-morrow may be a step which, if taken at all, should be taken with great caution. Speaking broadly, however, were we face to face with the electorate to-morrow I should not hesitate to say that, having regard to adjustments here and there, of which account would of necessity have to be taken, the Liberal party if returned to office would restore the tariff structure of this country to levels at least the equivalent of those which existed when we went out of office. What Canada requires above all else to-day is a policy which will be more concerned with encouraging exports than with keeping out imports.
Then in the South Huron by-election the Prime Minister repeated what he said at Winnipeg:
I want to say at once that the Liberal party in Canada has never at any time had a belief in the efficacy of high tariffs. Our view is that economic conditions not only permit but demand with respect to world trade an immediate substantial general reduction in customs duties, and for the purposes of greater freedom of trade within the British Empire no uncertain increase in the British preference.
I would repeat to-day what I said' at Winnipeg before the opening of the last session of parliament-that the Canadian tariff should be brought immediately to the level of what it was at the time the Liberal party went out of office in 1930; in other words to a level the equivalent of that established by the Dunning budget.
This was not only the declaration of the leader of the Liberal party; it was the policy of the Liberal party as a whole. This policy was put clearly before the people in every part of Canada from coast to coast. One of the reasons why I support this trade agreement strongly is that it is in accord with Liberal

Canada-UJS. Trade Agreement
policy; it is a step in the right direction The Canadian people will greet this as a first step, with other steps to follow; they will accept this agreement with the United States as a first instalment in redemption of the pledge given to them by the Liberal party.
Our policy with regard to the tariff is twofold; we believe in making trade agreements on a reciprocal basis with all countries that are willing to trade with us, and we hope that this trade agreement is the first of many similar ones that will be negotiated by the Canadian government. I should like to see the government commence immediately negotiations with Russia with a view to concluding a trade agreement with that country. I believe we could make with Russia a trade agreement that would be of advantage to that country and decidedly advantageous to Canada. We could buy from Russia oil and coal, and we could sell to her machinery and manufactured goods. Great Britain has made a trade agreement with Russia. There is nothing dangerous in making such an agreement, and we should at once embark upon an investigation of the possibilities of concluding a trade agreement with that country.
Might I ask the hon. member what party it was that broke off trade relationships with Russia?

I do not think that has anything to do with the present discussion. We in common with others suffered from the insanity of economic nationalism, but it is my hope that we are emerging from that insanity-
Hear, hear.

-and are now upon the pathway towards a sound economic policy.
I think we could make a trade agreement with Germany. Mr. James Richardson after being there indicated that he had heard many expressions of opinion in that country to the effect that they would be willing to buy Canadian wheat if we were ready to buy German goods. And we could make trade agreements with a number of other countries. I have personal knowledge that the small country of Iceland, from which my parents came, would be very glad indeed to make a trade agreement with Canada. Might I digress for a moment and on behalf of the people of Iceland thank both the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition for their splendid efforts in bringing about on the occasion of the one thousandth anniversary of parliament in Iceland a presentation to that country of a scholarship fund. I am sure that no gift from Canada to the people of Iceland could have been more welcome.
Our policy should be one of trade. Our wealth can be increased only by the exchange of goods, and a policy whereby there will be an exchange of goods is essential to a return to prosperity. Any persons or any party who preach that we cannot build up an exchange of goods preach a defeatist policy.
Our tariff policy is not confined to the making of trade treaties. If we can get concessions from other countries, well and good; we accept them gladly. But it is the view of a great number of people in Canada who have suffered from the high tariff policies of the previous administration, that we should make substantial and immediate reductions in the tariff, whether we get corresponding concessions from other countries or not.
Practically the whole of the argument of the right hon. gentleman opposite was directed to his contention that we did not get adequate consideration from the United States in respect of the concessions we gave that country. If I were to have any quarrel with the trade agreement now before us it would be that we have not sufficiently lowered our own tariff. We do not regard the tariff as an instrument to be used exclusively for bargaining purposes. The right hon. gentleman asked: What else have we to bargain with? Heaven knows that a tariff which still reaches over 200 per cent protection, in some instances, leaves ample room for reduction, whether such reduction be brought about as a result of reciprocal trade treaties or as a consequence of unilateral reductions in the tariff.
There are many people in Canada who are not satisfied with the reductions which have already taken place. The Canadian people are demanding a lower tariff, in the interests of both primary producers and consumers. They are not satisfied with the tariff reductions that have already been made. The debate in committee of ways and means will show the outrageous protection still in force; there are numerous commodities on which the people of Canada are undoubtedly demanding substantial tariff reductions. For instance, they want reductions on oil, gasoline, agricultural implements and textiles. There are many of us who feel that we must lower the costs of production and the cost of living. The primary producer has had to accommodate himself to world prices. In this country we cannot continue to bonus every form of production, as we have been attempting to do. Such a course of procedure is artificial and ruinous. We must restore the balance between prices of agricultural products and those of manufactured goods, and that balance can be brought about only by tariff reductions. Industry would not suffer as a
Copyright Act-Mr. Esling

result of such reductions. The whole country would gain through increased volume of trade, and the resulting increased purchasing power of the consumer.
One of the curses in Canada lies in the monopolies which have been developed. It is our duty to break up concentrations of wealth and these monopolies and, as best we can, to bring about a fair policy of competition, with no special privileges.
The Canadian people have spoken in an emphatic and distinct voice. They have voiced their discontent; they have given a mandate to the Liberal party, and to-day that party is on trial. As Liberals it is our duty to obey the wishes of our people and to carry out the mandate entrusted to us. I support this resolution as strongly as possible, believing we are beginning a new era of international trade, based upon principles of international good will and mutual advantage, and that we are witnessing the inauguration of a fiscal' policy suited to the needs of the Canadian people and designed to promote their welfare.
On motion of Mr. Thorson, the debate was adjourned.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
