Mr. W. K. ESLING (Kootenay West) moved the second reading of Bill No. 7, to amend the Copyright Amendment Act, 1931.
He said; Mr. Speaker, the suggestion aws that the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) might go home to celebrate his natal anniversary this evening, and as this bill comes under his department it was my intention to let it stand until the next sitting, but inasmuch as the minister is here, I think we might as well proceed.
There is one primary thought which ought to be remembered by members in the con-

sideration of this bill, and that is that the work and achievement and the genius of an author or composer are his own personal property, and it must be protected just as much as a vested right in real estate. The author or composer has a claim to an indefeasible title to anything he produces.
I think the next fact to be considered is that the public must pay for the production of music. Canada was a signatory to the Berne convention and by virtue of that fact our Canadian authors and composers are protected in other countries just as the authors and composers of other countries are protected in Canada. So there are two phases of this copyright act which must be borne in mind.
The operations of the Canadian Performing Right Society became so reckless, shall I say, as to become, well, nothing short of a racket; so much so that complaints were made to the Secretary of State and it was deemed wise to appoint a royal commissioner to make a thorough investigation of this society. I am very glad that the Secretary of State has furnished the members wfth a copy of the report of His Honour Judge Parker because, Mr. Speaker, there is no use discussing a bill unless the members are fully informed on their topic. The operations of the Canadian Performing Right Society are a matter of vital interest to every community, large and small, in this dominion, and therefore of vital importance to every member who desires to serve his community.
This question goes back to the amendment to the copyright act that was made in 1931, where authority was given to companies controlling copyright to issue licences and collect fees from those who performed music in public. I repeat that when that amendment was made it expressed the unanimous voice of the house because the general intention was that the amendment was for the protection of Canadian authors, composers and publishers. The very name of the society bears that out-the Canadian Performing Right Society. But as a matter of fact we find that Canadian authors and composers do not participate in or benefit by the collection of these licence fees in any way whatsoever.
The Canadian Performing Right Society, as I stated on the first reading of this bill, was the outcome of some genius in the United States or England. In the United States the American Society of Authors, Composers and Publishers exists, and in England there is the Performing Right Society of England, with which are affiliated similar societies in other countries, all signatories to the Berne con-
FEBRUARY 28, 1936	f
Copyright Act-Mr. Chevrier (Ottawa)
vention, and they are all authorized under the authority of their respective countries to issue licences and to collect fees.
Throughout the Dominion of Canada every broadcasting station, every theatre, every radio in a hotel or restaurant and every public hall of any kind, whether it be a fraternity or community hall, every place in which music is played for public purposes, is called upon to pay a licence fee under the amendment to section 10 of the 1931 copyright act. The Canadian Performing Right Society is composed, as I stated on the first reading, of the American company, the English company and some eighteen European companies. They have not very much of a financial set up in Canada, the capital structure consisting of 10,000 no par value shares, and only two shares are held in Canada. The directors are resident three in the United States, one in England, and two provisional directors in Toronto.
Moreover, there is no limit, it seems, to the licence fee they can charge. When they commenced their operations they fixed the minimum charge at S10 per year for every hotel, restaurant, and public hall, but in January, 1935, they arbitrarily raised that minimum from $10 to $30. Now the point is this, that there is nothing to prevent them from raising the rates much higher again. They have already made this arbitrary raise of the minimum from $10 to $30. as I have mentioned, and also in January, 1935, they raised the rate on theatres from a minimum of ten cents a seat to 15 and 20 cents a seat. Many of the larger theatres have not paid that higher rate because they can afford to fight any attempt at extortion, but the little fellows cannot afford to hire lawyers, and through fear and threats pay the fee, whether they believe it to be excessive or not. The theatres in 1934 paid this Canadian Performing Right Society, the company in which there are no Canadians participating at all, the sum of $50,000, and in 1935 the rate to the theatres was raised The radio broadcasting stations paid to the Canadian Performing Right Society approximately $63,000 in 1934, and in 1935 that was raised approximately to $83,000. The hotel and radio fees were doubled from $25,000 to $50,000 in 1935.
There is also the fact that any other society in Canada can, under section 10 of the copyright act, 1931, go out and levy a similar toll. There is nothing in the world to prevent two or three or four or as many companies as you please from incorporating and collecting these tolls, and their minimum fee may be ten or twenty or thirty dollars.
The present company rule entirely by threats, and the fear which they instil in the hearts of the small theatre owners compels them to pay. Only to-day I had a communication from a law firm in regard to the case of a little fellow who had been trying to create some amusement for the people at the beach. With his own hands he spent two and a half months building a hall, and at the end of the season, after the cottagers had left, along came the Canadian Performing Right Society collector, demanding $30, or more money than the boy had taken in. He paid it out of fear and had practically nothing left for his work.
Throughout British Columbia the Canadian Performing Right Society, apparently fearing that this investigation by Judge Parker would result in legislation which would curb their operations, sent men into the field collecting money here, there and everywhere, wherever they could get it. If any fraternal society refused to pay the $30 as required they would come back and take $20 or $10 or anything they could get.
I have introduced this bill in the hope that there will be a full and free discussion on the part of all hon. members so that something may be done to curb what can be nothing but a means .of extorting money from the Canadian public.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. R. E. CHEVRIER (Ottawa East):
speechtext:
The main reason I rise on this occasion is that we are concerned with the second reading of this bill; and, according to the practice that prevails in this house, whoever allows the passing of the second reading is regarded as a matter of course as assenting to the principle of the bill.
My stand on this matter goes back fifteen years in the house, and you, Mr. Speaker, and some of the other members, are familiar with my views regarding copyright. This evening I desire to approach this question from one point only, namely, the question of rights. It is well known that we are now a party to the convention of Berne. There are two classes of authors: those who are our own nationals and those who belong to nations which are parties to the Beme convention and are neither Canadians nor Canadian nationals. So far as our own nationals are concerned, we may violate the convention of Berne from the first to the last letter; we may stultify ourselves by proclaiming any arbitrary measure to the detriment of our own nationals, and. it is up to our own authors to suffer. But as adherents to the Berne convention we have

642	COMMONS
Copyright Act

Mr. Chevrier (Ottawa)
to respect that international undertaking, and under the terms of that convention copyright exists in every one of the countries that are participants in the convention, and that without any formality whatsoever. As regards all works, whether literary or artistic, no formality need be complied with to secure copyright. The ownership in the copyright may be in the author or it may be in his assignee, and as the hon. gentleman who is proposing the bill (Mr. Esling) has said, the right to the copyright must be respected just as much as is a title to real estate.
Unfortunately in Canada that is not so. Those who in the past have been charged with the elaboration of a copyright act have always and to this moment neglected to protect the copyright holder. The most glaring evidence of that was given before one of the committees of the house when a gentleman from Toronto came to give evidence and declared that he represented the Copyright Protective Association. On examination of that witness it was found that the shareholders and those who composed the Copyright Protective Association were paper makers, dealers in twine, dealers in paste, and dealers in ink and typesetting, but there was not a single owner of a copyright nor was there one author in that corporation. We have neglected to safeguard the rights of authors.
For many years we have been endeavouring to provide remedies and to afford some measure of protection, but the law as it now stands is a fearful testimony to the monumental lack of protection. With reference to these two kinds of authors, we may do as we please with our own nationals; but as regards those who are not Canadian nationals, they retain their right to copyright and have a perfect right to charge whatever they may wish to exact in connection with the performance or reproduction of their works, whether literary or artistic. I protested vigorously in the name of these outside authors when this law was enacted. True, I recognize that there must not be a monopoly; true, these artistic or literary works may be reproduced for the good of the community. But after all the authors have a perfect right to say whether for So or S50 or for nothing at all their works may be reproduced.
It may be objected that in the patent law the ownership is taken away after a certain length of time. There may be some difference as 'between copyright in a piece of music and a patent on a wonderful instrument or an improvement, whether in connection with

the telephone, the telegraph, the Marconi system or some of the most recent developments of science. There may be something in that. But there is no particular reason why the rights of composers to fees should be taken away from them and should be given some arbitrary compensation.
Is there any real reason why there should be a corporation called the Performing Right Society? I am not at all concerned with the Performing Right Society. As to whether it exists I am not concerned in the slightest degree. But it will be recognized at once that authors belonging to those nations of Europe and of other parts of the world subscribing to the Berne convention cannot very 'well supervise the collection of their own fees in Canada, any more than Canadian authors can supervise the collection of royalties in Japan, Belgium, France, Switzerland, Italy and other countries that are adherents to the convention. Some association must exist for the collection of these fees. I have not gone into the question, but it may be a fact that in the Performing Right Society there are no Canadians who have assigned to that corporation any of their rights. Nevertheless there are authors and copyright holders, assignees of those rights, who have handed over to that corporation the collection of their fees. I am not suggesting for a moment that the Canadian Performing Right Society should have the right to charge something outrageous, but we are faced with this problem:	We belong to the convention
of Berne or we do not. We have signed that international convention' we are bound to adhere to its tenets, and I submit that we cannot by this means interfere with the rights and the royalties of those authors and composers and assignees thereof who are not nationals. It is all very well to say that there is a racket-probably there is; I am not concerned for the moment whether there is or not-and to say that enormous fees are being charged. But I think that what was shown under past circumstances is well within the memory of any hon. member who has sat in the house for some years.
I did not intend to speak on this matter this evening, but I collected just at random one or two items from a most voluminous collection of documents that I happen to have, and if I am allowed I shall cite one or two of them. It was disclosed before the committee on railways and shipping on June 24, 1931, with reference to Canadian National broadcasting that the total amount paid for talent in 1930 was 895,073.82. This was for the artists who performed the copyrighted works; 195,000 was paid to the per-

Copyright Act-Mr. Chevrier (Ottawa)
formers of those compositions. And when I asked this question in the house on July 2, 1931:
What amount of money was paid by the Canadian National Railway Company to authors and composers of copyrighted music and of other works, as fees or royalties for the use of the said copyrighted music or other works by the said Canadian National Railways broadcasting stations in Canada during the past twelve months?
-the period corresponding to that within which $95,073.82 had been paid for talent- I was answered by the then Minister of Railways that the sum paid in copyrights was the magnificent one of $20.42. The authors obtained $20.42 in order that those who performed those copyrighted works might obtain $95,073.82, and for rentals the additional sum of $60,756.23. I leave it to hon. members to say, first, whether a racket exists, and, second, where the racket does exist; whether the author derives a comparable benefit for the work which he puts on the market.
Going back to the 1931 committee I recall the evidence of Mr. Gitz Rice. If there is any racket let us see where it is. He said, at page 78 of the report of the committee's proceedings on June 30, 1931:
Since I started my profession of song writing I have been very fortunate in writing some of the world' war's greatest songs. I have yet to collect the first cent from my own country, Canada, for them.
And further down he says:
The composer always gets the worst of it, no matter where you go.
And he adds:
At the same time the Victor Berliner Company of Montreal, published 250,000 records of McCormack singing "Dear Old Pal of Mine,"-
-written by Mr. Gitz Rice-
-and never paid me a cent.
It is with those two views in mind that I approach this question. The first one is, as I have said, that under the terms of the convention of Berne we may do as we please with our own people; we may humiliate them to our hearts' satisfaction by not allowing them to get any of the fees and royalties to which they are entitled, but at the same time I say that so long as we are participants in the convention of Berne we cannot arbitrarily determine what the compensation or royalties shall be to those who are not nationals.
In passing I may say that we have placed ourselves through our copyright law in a very bad light so far as European countries are concerned. In the last few years I have received a large number of comments upon our law, and I am afraid that some of them, ex-12739- 4li
pressed by leading lawyers and jurisconsults of the continent, would be hardly parliamentary. I have under my hand one from M. Francois Hepp, who is a Doctor of Law in Paris. What he says is this:
Un texte legislatif important, et qui ne peut sembler aux amis du "Droit d'Auteur" que vraiment bizarre (sinon monstrueux), a ete vote, le 17 avril 1935, en troisieme lecture.
A free translation of that is:
An important legislative .text, which may seem to the friends of "Droit d'Auteur" nothing less than peculiar (if not monstrous) was voted on third reading on April 17, 1935, by the Canadian Senate.
That in effect is what leading experts on copyright law say of our present Canadian copyright act.
I suggest that there should be a complete revision of that act, with a view of doing exactly what its title says, making it an act for the protection of copyright and not an act for the protection of everything but copyright. If we go back to the origins of the law -I am not going to trace them-whether common law or statute law, we shall find that in those countries where people were moved by the fairness of the right of the copyright holder, be he composer or author, justice was done to him; also that justice has not been done to our Canadian authors and composers. I shall give but one illustration of the sacredness of copyright, going back to the very earliest times of the colony. I remember reading in the Relations of the Jesuit Fathers that an Indian had his own war song and that nobody else was allowed to sing it; if some one did so it was the right of the one whose copyright had been infringed to engage in warfare and to kill that person if he could. So that copyright goes as far back as the Indians of the earliest days of the colony, and I deplore the fact that even to this day Canadian authors do not enjoy, not the right of life and death over their infringers, but a fair measure of security.
I understand that the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) proposes at a later date to introduce a bill to implement in some respects the report of Judge Parker. This is neither the time nor the place to discuss that report but I am very much afraid that we shall be faced again with the same situation, namely, trying to determine rights in respect of something over which we have no jurisdiction whatever. It may be true that monopolies exist in Canada as regards the collection of these fees, but I pointed out on another occasion that the place to deal with the matter was not on copyright legislation. There is another statute the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, and
Copyright Act-Mr. Cahan

if we must do something by legislation, why not place that provision in the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act and take it out of the copyright act. No other copyright legislation in the world contains such a provision. The place to have it, if you must have it, is outside the statute altogether.
I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, again to say that when the matter arises at a later date either in committee or on the third reading, I shall declare my complete opposition to anything which infringes the conditions under which we entered into the convention of Berne. With all deference I say that the government would be well advised to wait until the next convention takes place in Brussels next September. Then, in the light of what takes place there, after a study .of the grievances that have been alleged against [DOT]our own system and after consultation with experts representing the various other countries, a measure can be framed which we can truly call a copyright act, which will contain the essential of copyright, which is the protection of the copyright owner.

I should like
to ask the hon. member if the Berne agreement protects against reproduction or against reception.
In the Canadian act there is a provision with reference to radio; I suppose that is what the hon. gentleman means. That applies the provisions of the Berne convention to reproduction by radio.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for
Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) has directed attention to evils that were persistently brought to the notice of the previous government. The hon. gentleman is entirely in error when he suggests that the copyright legislation of 1931 first authorized the owners of musical copyrights to license the performing rights in such copyright. That authorization has existed for many years.
The legislation of 1931 was directed to the regulation and control of such associations and companies as had acquired musical copyrights, and were exercising those rights by making utterly unjust demands upon the public for the use of their performing rights. I know the hon. member for East Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) has some very strong views on the matter. From time to time he has presented them before this house and before .several of the committees of this house, but neither in the committees nor in the house has he obtained legislative recognition of those views.
XMr. E. R. E. Chevrier.]
During the last session these evils became so apparent that it became necessary for the government to appoint a commission to make a judicial inquiry into the facts in order to ascertain whether and to what extent these allegations of monopoly and unjust price were founded in fact. The amendment of last year, therefore, had in view the appointment of such a commission. That legislation passed, I think, without dissent; certainly, as far as I remember, it passed without dissent from the hon. member for Ottawa East, and at an early date the government did appoint a royal commission to make the inquiry.
I have read cursorily the report of that commission; I know from the newspaper reports that the investigation was a long and exhaustive one. I know the various interests were represented there by some of the ablest counsel that could be procured in Canada, and there these questions were fought out. If the government of which I was formerly a member had remained in office I have no doubt that on the recommendation of the Secretary of State, after an investigation had been held, either by order in council, as authorized under the act, or by legislation, some real effort would have been made to regulate or suppress the evils which had grown up. This is a matter with which the government must deal, I think, as a government, simply because in dealing with it the government must comply with the obligations which this country has undertaken by becoming a party to the Berne convention. That convention was signed by the preceding government of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and the duty and obligation was placed upon the succeeding government, which was the late government, of seeing to it that the convention was conserved, but also that any evils which had grown up, under the organization of a Canadian company called the Canadian Performing Right Society, Limited, should be mitigated and if possible restrained.
Undoubtedly, I think, under the Berne convention this parliament has a right to deal with radio communication, and under that convention there is no restriction upon our right to enforce criminal and quasicriminal measures. Under the Berne convention there is no restriction to our right to put an end to price-fixing and extortion such as has been alleged in connection with the Canadian Performing Right Society, Limited. I will not say that this was founded on fact, because I have not had an opportunity of reading the evidence which was heard by the commission; that evidence was returned to

Copyright Act-Mr. Rinjret
the Secretary of State after I left office, and this government must now deal with that matter. We have had an assurance by the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) that this government will deal with the matter, and I think we may feel confident that a matter of this kind will be dealt with effectively.
Therefore I would suggest to the hon. mem-er for Kootenay West either that he have this debate adjourned until such time as it can be ascertained whether or not the measures proposed by the government are effective, or that this bill be withdrawn as premature. The evils cannot be dealt with as the hon. member for West Kootenay has attempted to deal with them in this measure; I am quite clear as to that. But that they can be dealt with under the recommendations, or some of the recommendations, made by the commissioner, who sat and heard evidence for months, I believe is possible, and therefore I think it would be far better to leave the government free to deal with these evils.

Mr. Speaker, I think even this short debate will have convinced the house that this matter of copyright is a very complex problem. In two successive speeches we have heard the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) contending that there is a racket in the matter of exacting fees in favour of the composers, and the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Chevrier), who quoted what he said was a celebrated jurist, contending that it is monstrous that the fees exacted should be so small and of so little benefit to the composers of music. 1 herefore I think I am safe in concurring in the statement made by my predecessor in office (Mr. Cahan) that strong views are entertained on both sides of the question, and that an effort should be made to reconcile those views and introduce legislation which will assure an even measure of justice.
As to the principle of the bill, I fully agree with the sponsor that it is desirable to give effect by legislation to the results of the inquiry made by Judge Parker. But we cannot dissociate this intention from the provisions of the bill which are known to us, and I completely disagree with him as to the methods by which he proposes that the house should follow up the report made by Judge Parker. I may not have time to go into details to-night, but I think it could easily be proved that in both respects he is completely in disagreement with Judge Parker. Inasmuch as my hon. friend has praised the appointment of a royal commission I believe he will be willing to support
the government when a bill is brought down that will embody more completely the recommendations made by Judge Parker.
In passing let me say that although I have on more than one occasion supported the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Chevrier) in his efforts to obtain a good copyright law-in this country, I am not in agreement with him on the point that is under discussion just now. This bill, the bill I shall bring in and the inquiry made by Judge Parker deal merely with the activities of the Canadian Performing Right Society, and I contend that this society has placed itself in a position where special measures are absolutely necessary to meet the situation. The society may own copyrights on foreign music, but it is a Canadian organization, very close to a monopoly, and I must say most decidedly, as the minister charged with the administration of copyright, that I consider its activities are distinctly in opposition to the in-< terests of true copyright as I understand it. I believe that if an individual composer of music takes advantage of the present law he can have the fullest protection, but when we have to deal with a monopoly, a society owning thousands or hundreds of thousands; of musical compositions, we certainly have-to adopt towards such a company special provisions in the act. The hon. member for Ottawa East himself agreed that that might be necessary, but he said: Why not do it by another act? In reply I say that if he is agreeable to have it in another act, why should he oppose having it in this one, because the effect will be the same, the result will be identical, whether we deal with that society by the copyright act or the Combines Investigation Act. All that the Canadian Performing Right Society does is to hold a monopoly on musical compositions and exact fees for the use of them. This is not copyright in the true sense of the word. We have never known how the money collected is distributed to the composers. I am still at a loss to find out how this is done. In dealing with this society we are facing not copyright but a special application of it, and personally I do not think there would be any conflict with the Berne convention in having special sections dealing, with this society.
What the former Secretary of State did was to have an act passed in 1931 forcing this society and others of the same character, if they exist, to file a statement of their fees with the Department of the Secretary of State, and if there was opposition or conflict over those fees the act provided for the appoint-
Copyright Act-Mr. Rinfret

ment of a commissioner to make inquiry. That is what was done, and we now have in our hands the report of Judge Parker, appointed a commissioner on March 22, 1935, to investigate the whole situation. I would say to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) that although he professes to follow the work of the commissioner, in both of the sections that he proposes, he has completely missed the point made by Judge Parker. In the first place my hon. friend wants to fix maximum fees for the performance of musical compositions either over the radio or in theatres or otherwise, and if there is anything that is very plain in the report of Judge Parker it is that he said that should be dealt with only on the actual situation. He does admit that the whole matter is in the experimental stage, and his chief proposal is:
That the copyright act be amended so as to provide for the establishment of an appeal tribunal, to determine disputes arising out of performance in public and to approve of the tariffs of the Canadian Performing Right Society, Limited, from time to time before they become effective.
In other words, far from recommending any permanent fee the recommendation of Judge Parker is that there should be a tribunal that would every year, if there is any discussion as to the fees filed in the Department of the Secretary of State, hear such appeals.
In the second section of my hon. friend's bill he proposes that the society should not only file a list of its musical compositions with the Department of the Secretary of State, but also furnish a copy of such list to hotels and restaurants and other places where such performances may be heard. On that point also he is in complete disagreement *with the report of Judge Parker, who at page 33 makes it very plain that he does not think the society may be in a position to file any complete list with the Secretary of State or to supply that list to every performer of the music. I agree with the hon. member for Kootenay West that there is some ground for the argument that if you do charge a fee on music the least you can do would be to tell the performer what music that is. The fact that they cannot supply lists shows conclusively that this society is a monopoly of a very special character and that we cannot deal with it in the same way as if it were a true and complete owner of copyrights in the real sense of the word.
The hon. member for Ottawa East has cited a case which is very pathetic, that of the composer of the famous song "Dear Old Pal of Mine." I think we all agree that that song was sung everywhere, not only in this country but in the United States, and that the com-
MV. Rinfret.]
poser did not have even the slight redress that could be exercised now in favour of a similar case. But I say again that if we had to deal with individual cases I would advocate that the law be made if possible more strict in favour of the composer. But I ask my hon. friend to consider that any bill we introduce must deal with the special case of the Canadian Performing Right Society, and that case cannot ibe dealt with in the same spirit or regulated in the same way as if we were dealing with individual composers.
I thank the former Secretary of State for the proposal he made, which I am also going to make to the mover of this bill, that he either let his bill stand or else withdraw it until the government through myself present to the house the bill that we have in mind. It is -not customary to disclose the contents of a bill before it is given first reading because, like everything else, it is subject to changes. I may say, however, that it is the intention of the government to present a bill which will follow closely the recommendations made by Mr. Justice Parker. The bill will tend to create a tribunal of appeal where, every year at a certain period, performers may appeal from the fees of the Canadian Performing Right Society, and other societies. We wish to observe the principle mentioned to-night by the hon. member for Ottawa East that the owner of the copyright in the first place should file a fee which he believes to be proper. Inasmuch as we have to deal with what I shall again describe as a monopoly, we also want to give to the performer the opportunity of coming before the tribunal each year at a certain date to appeal from the fees fixed or registered in my department by such societies. I think we should preserve both principles, that of the free ownership of a copyright and, at the same time, that of regulating against a monopoly wherever it exists.
Further, it will be necessary to provide for the transition period between the time Mr. Justice Parker was appointed and the time the new bill will be in operation. A bill was passed in 1935 covering the circumstances, whereby no action may be taken in the recovery of fees pending the inquiry. But from the time that Mr. Justice Parker was appointed until the time the new bill will be in effect, and, if we provide for a tribunal, until the time when the appeal would have been heard by that tribunal, it will be necessary to cover the transition period. That will have to be done by the Secretary of State with the consent of parliament. Provision will be made therefor in the incoming bill.

Dominion Franchise Act
Supported by the Secretary of State of the late administration-and I again thank him for his support because we happen to be of the same mind-I renew my request to have the hon. member's consent to let the bill stand, and not force second reading. If he should do otherwise I would have to vote against it.

It seems to me that protection of copyright lies within the whole field of reproduction, and not that of reception. I hope the government is taking that point into consideration. It seems to me ridiculous that the owner of a radio receiving set should be compelled to pay for everything he receives.

There is
nothing in the act about that.
On motion of Mr. Neill the debate was adjourned.

Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Dominion Franchise Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I crave the indulgence of the house to speak again, as this bill comes under my jurisdiction. I believe the provisions in the bill are self-explanatory and should not prove contentious. The object of the bill is simply to postpone for one year the revision of the existing lists. As hon. members are aware a committee of the house has been agreed upon and will soon be formed to study amendments to the elections act and the Dominion Franchise Act. Many proposals have come from different sources respecting amendments to the electoral law.
In the debate on the address several hon. members referred to changes which should be made in our electoral law. Further references have been made in the press and in private correspondence indicating a strong desire to amend the elections act and the Dominion Franchise Act. Under the circumstances the postponement of the annual revision to take place this year seemed the obvious procedure. There is no desire to cast any reflection upon the existing law. My own experience has been that it has worked very well in more than one particular, and I pay my respects to the former government in its execution of this legislation. I may say that the law has functioned well in the district in which I happened to live during election time, and there is not the least desire to cast any reflections upon the law when, in the name of the government, I propose the postponement of the revision.
I would bring to the attention of the house the fact, in the first place, that a revision is very costly. A question on the order paper has asked for the full costs of preparing the lists for the last general election, a procedure which of course was quite necessary, and for the costs in connection with the revision which took place last May.
So that hon. members may have the facts may I say that when the dominion franchise commissioner placed his estimates before me he had two sets of proposals. If there was to be no revision he was satisfied with a sum of about $16,000, but if there was to be a revision he asked for $350,000. Hon. members will understand that these expenditures are very great. It is my opinion that in the city ridings, at least, the revision would bring very small results. It is not likely that electors would be anxious to attend before a revising officer, because the election is far away, and the incentive for attendance is lacking. I do not believe many hon. members would be in favour of spending a huge sum of money upon a revision at this time. Were we to have a revision we would have to pay a high price for it, and probably get only small results.
The only reason, however, from the administrative point of view, which has governed the submission of the bill is that we are likely to have amendments to the electoral law before the end of the present session. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has pointed out-and his observations have been approved by many hon. members-that it is better to amend the electoral law at the first session of a new parliament than to wait until the closing session. I confidently expect that before the session is over a new electoral law may be considered. The necessity for moving this bill at this time is that, if circumstances had not been foreseen and some provision made, the printing bureau already would be printing forms for the next revision, and by April 1 notice would be given in the Canada Gazette by the dominion franchise officer to the different revising officers throughout the country to prepare for the revision. That is why I ask the house to pass this bill now as an emergency measure. It does not propose to deal with the situation at all in a full way; it is merely to prevent the pending revision taking place and pos-
Dominion Franchise Act

sibly then coming into conflict with some new electoral law and some new forfn of preparation of the lists. I think the object of the bill is obvious, and I do not think I need say any more at the moment.
['On what basis could you make the estimate?\nProgress reported.']

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext: Having had experience for five years in dealing with the elections act and the franchise act, and in view of the proposed amendments to both these acts, I certainly agree with the hon. gentleman that the pending revision should be deferred.

Mr. Speaker, I rise not for the purpose of objection to the principle of this bill because as the government does not expect a general election in the next year I think it is quite proper that we should avoid the expense to the country at large and to the parties responsible for the revision of the list of an annual revision now. There is, however, one situation which I desire to bring to the attention of the government, and that is the possibility of a byelection being held. Under the provisions of the act as it now stands, the list that is in force will continue to be the list until another is prepared, and if revision is done away within the year 1936 there could not be another revision before
1937.	It would not be complete until July 1, 1937, and then there would be the printing after that. If we had a byelection at any time within the next six months we would be voting on the line of the list that was made in the year 1935, and so I suggest that the government might well consider putting into this measure a section providing that in case of a byelection being held the governor in council would have power to authorize and direct a revision or an enumeration which would bring up to date the list in that electoral constituency. I think we will all agree that it is desirable that the electoral lists should be up to date, and in these days when people are moving about, particularly from city to city, a list a year old would be very much out of date. That is the only suggestion I have to make, that the government consider inserting in this bill a provision that in the case of a byelection being held the governor in council would have power to order a revision or an enumeration in the constituency concerned.
If my hon. friend will agree we might take up that point in committee.
That is quite satisfactory, Mr. Speaker.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Annual revision of lists.
['That is quite satisfactory, Mr. Speaker.']

Mr. Chairman, I must say that I had foreseen the remarks that were made by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) because I took up that very question with the dominion franchise commissioner when we were preparing this bill. My hon. friend's point I think is well taken. I will agree with him as to that. Byelections, of course, are governed by section 18, which governs all elections, whether byelections or general elections. It reads as follows:
The lists of electors which shall be made and certified pursuant to this part of this act shall be valid until revised lists, replacing and superseding them, shall have been made and certified pursuant to part III of this act.
My hon. friend is quite right when he says that if this act is passed and nothing further is done in the meantime, any byelection taking place this year will be held on the lists as they actually exist, but on the other hand it did not seem possible to include in this bill a provision such as he suggests unless we created entirely new machinery altogether, because the whole of part III of the bill is based upon the fact that notice is given on the first of April that certain things shall take place on certain dates, and the revision goes on in a certain fixed way. In other words, if we could foresee in advance what byelections are coming, we might say that these sections would apply only in the case of certain counties, but I may say that we have not found it possible to include in the bill a section which would make the act operative only in certain cases, and in order to cover the case of a byelection we would have to revise a long list of sections just to cover that eventuality.
As the government was confident that it might be possible to have a new act passed this session we thought we would in the meantime ask the house to pass this bill as it stands, merely for the purpose of stopping immediately the oncoming revision. I repeat that I see the point that has been made by my hon. friend. Perhaps we might agree that if the amendments to the electoral laws are not available this year, which is in the nature of a possibility, we might still before the end of this session find a way of meeting the special case my hon. friend mentions, but We have not considered the question of a single section foreseeing the eventuality of a bylection because, as I have pointed out, the

Dominion Franchise Act
whole act is framed in a very definite way providing for annual revisions to take place at certain dates and under certain conditions. If the committee will agree to let the bill pass as it stands I will undertake to deal with the special case brought forward by my hon. friend.

As I understand the
situation, the proceedings in connection with the annual revision will not take place until April 1, which is more than a month away, so no expenditure would be incurred in the meantime. I have not looked into the matter perhaps as carefully as has the Secretary of State, but I am inclined to think it would not be difficult to draft a section or two or three sections which would in themselves provide for the contingency of byelections. We are facing one now. The Speaker announced to-night a vacancy in one of the constituencies, and that he had issued his writ.
That would be held under the old list.

Exactly, and I think
it is undesirable that an election should be held on a list that is a year old. It will be considerably more than a year old when the election is held. All our elections in recent years have been based upon a list that is brought thoroughly up to date through the medium of an enumeration. It seems to me that it could be provided that in case of a byelection enumerators should be appointed and that they should perform the duties set out in section so and so for the purpose of that byelection. I do not think there is any difficulty whatever in drafting an amendment to cover the point which we have in view, and which the Secretary of State admits is important and well taken. It seems to me that we might leave the bill in committee for a day or so until we see whether we cannot work out something of that kind. I do not want to delay the bill at all, and I do not want to cause the incurring of any expense which can be avoided, but the revision would not, in any event, start until April.

We have had for a number of years one or other of the systems of preparing lists, either that of preparing lists on the eve of an election at the last moment, or this system which provides for a fixed or permanent list revised once a year. I say again that it would require practically a new act to provide for byelections in the manner suggested. by the hon. gentleman. I do not see how it would be possible to amend this act in that regard at all; we should have to repeal the whole of part III dealing with the preparation of lists and bring in a new
bill altogether. And that might conflict with another measure which is likely to be presented to the house before we prorogue.
I would point out that until July any byelection held would have to be staged on the lists as they are, because until that time the new lists would not have been printed, at least not until the first of July, which is the ultimate date of revision. The hon. gentleman's objection was foreseen and we came to the conclusion that the immediate urgency was merely to postpone revision, because there will be time later in the session to consider the question of providing for byelections.
I have stated and I state again that even if this bill had not been on the order paper the printing bureau would be already printing for the revision and the entire machinery would ibe set in motion within a few weeks, and that is what we want to stop. We are asking the approval of the house of this bill, which we desire to send to the senate in time to prevent that machinery from being set in motion. Even if my hon. friend insisted on his point, I should still deem it necessary to have this bill passed, with an opportunity, if it were thought desirable, of introducing a bill dealing with byelections. In the meantime, however, I confidently trust that the committee will report this bill in time to make provision for an adequate electoral law during the present session. But if that were not done there would still be time to provide for a bill dealing with byelections.
My hon. friend has made another point, that unless what he suggests is done we shall not have revised lists until 1937. But that is the case under the present act, because the act as it stands at present provides for permanent lists. If we are to deal with byelections, however, I should be in favour of introducing a bill providing for special revision on the eve of a byelection, but that would be different altogether from the one that now exists. I appreciate the fact that electoral laws are a matter of compromise, but I think we are justified in asking the house to dispose of this point, and we can still consider the question of meeting my hon. friend's views with regard to byelections.

I do not want to seem
to be pressing this matter unduly, but the Secretary of State is dealing with general elections rather than with the point I am raising with respect to byelections, and I think he must admit it is not desirable that even a byelection should be held on a list which is a year old. He speaks about introducing legislation aimed at changing the
Dominion Franchise Act

whole of the act. That will probably not be introduced until near the end of the session; it is in many respects a contentious subject. In the meantime we might safeguard the situation; if we are to repeal the provision with respect to annual revision we really ought to make some provision with respect to byelections.

I support the suggestion of the hon. member for Leeds. I listened to what the minister said with regard to byelections, and perhaps I might make a few remarks with regard to a riding in Toronto in which there are approximately 60,000 people. On the lists upon which the election was held in October last I presume that out of that 60,000 there were 40,000 names listed. I am not sure, but that is an estimate. Of these, 9.000 families or persons had moved away. The election was in a riding in which there were a great many apartments; there are many university student rooming houses in the district. When the enumerators went through the riding and found that 9,000 families or persons had moved away, they did not strike the names off, so that when the election was held there were on the list 9000 names of people who did not vote. On the same list approximately one per cent of the names represented those who had died and it was said that not less than 1,000 names appeared twice on the list, names of people who had moved from one part of the riding to another. A number of names were on the list three times and I heard of one name that appeared four times. The enumerators had gotten the names in the fall of 1934 and they got them again in April, May or June in 1935. In the meantime these people had moved but their names were kept on. If the revision were made immediately before a byelection in Toronto this spring I am of the opinion that it would be found that twenty-five per cent of the names on a list were names that should have been struck off either because the people had moved away, or because the names were repeated or because the voters had died.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
May I point out that even if the present amendment were not introduced the inconveniences referred to by the two hon. members would exist. Under the act as it is now, without the amendment introduced by the Secretary of State, no new list can be ready until some time after the first of July, and it will be probably the first of August before it is printed. So that no matter what happened, the byelection now pending to which my hon. friend refers 
would be conducted under the law as it was passed in 1934 and on the list which came into effect on the first of July, 1935. No other list can come into effect until the first of July, 1936, unless some amendment is proposed in this house, so that what my hon. friends are asking for is an amendment to the act of 1934. They are asking for an amendment of that kind right now. The whole act is about to be revamped by the elections committee which will doubtless study the question whether the system of closed lists now in force, which entails the inconveniences that have been pointed out, shall continue to be the system to be followed, ;or whether it will be advisable in future to revert to the procedure followed under the 1930 act and the acts prior thereto, whereby a revision was made just after the writs were issued.
I understand that a large number of hon. members, having given the so-called closed list a trial and the fixed list a trial, desire to revert to the other system. That cannot be done without an amendment to the act, and what is being pressed to-night simply postpones the revision and leaves the way open for further discussion of the two methods of procedure, whether we are to have a closed list or an open list. I have not the slightest doubt that if the matter is pressed by the members and the committee makes due diligence it will be possible before the end of this session, and in plenty of time to meet the objections of my hon. friends- that is to say before July 1, 1936-to introduce some amendment whereby any election taking place after July 1, 1936, will be governed somewhat along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). So that if this particular amendment passes now, the committee could get to work at once and lay down some system of procedure, even if it were only a preliminary or an emergency measure, which would be in effect for an election prior to the time that a new election act is introduced.

I think if the act were left as it is there would be no complaint in connection with any byelection, because the list would not be too old. But when you come to amend the act and take away the only existing provision and make no provision for a byelection you are sure to have an old list. In the case of the byelection we have in mind I am sure the government would not fix the date of that byelection before July 1 if they felt that the act should remain exactly as it is, and the revision would be complete

Supply-External Affairs
by that time. But with this amendment they know perfectly well that there will be no revision; that the list will not be brought up to date even though they hold the byelection next fall. Six months may elapse from the date of the vacancy before they issue the writ, and if they took that time there would be under this amendment no new list, and be no revision of the list. Whereas if the act were left as it is, in due time there would be a new list, and the government could see to it that the byelection was held on the new list. On the other hand, if this amendment goes through, and no provision as suggested is made, they are depriving themselves of the power of holding a byelection on a list that is up to date.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As the case stands, any byelection prior to July next will have to be held under this act of 1935, whether we act on this bill or not. Would it solve the difficulty if I made this suggestion- after all, this session, I hope, is not going to last all summer-that when the end of the session comes in May or in June, and if it is apparent to everybody that there will be no change in the election law or in the franchise act as a result of the work of the committee that is going to sit, it would then be time enough to meet the objection of my hon. friends and have an act put upon the statutes to deal with any byelection which may take place after July 1 until next year? Would that solve the difficulty?
If the Minister of Justice on behalf of the government would intimate that that will be done, that will be quite satisfactory to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I may ask the government to do it, if my hon. friend is satisfied.

I hope the committee did not get the impression that I am opposed to the bill. I am not, and I am strongly in favour of a revision of the franchise act. All I want to be sure of is that this matter will be attended to in the event of a foyelection being held in a city riding. I do not think my objections would have the same weight with regard to a byelection held in a rural riding in the next few months, because lists do not change in the latter with anything like the same rapidity that they do in a city riding. But if a byelection were held in Montreal or Toronto within a month or two, it would make a great deal of difference whether the lists were to be revised or not. That is all I had in mind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is an increase of $13,271. May I say that $10,000 of this amount is to enable the office to be organized in a more businesslike manner than obtains at the moment. It is for purposes of administration. May I repeat what I said a year or two ago, namely, that a Prime Minister goes into his office with but one or two secretaries; he is not in the position of other ministers of the crown who enter well organized departments, headed by a deputy minister, and supplied with secretaries of the department and staff as well as personal secretaries. He may find a few stenographic clerks in the office of the Prime Minister, but for the whole administration of his office he is practically dependent upon the services of two or three private secretaries.
I believe my right hon. friend opposite will agree that it is really impossible to carry on the business of the Prime Minister's office without more adequate and effective administrative machinery. Above all else it seems to me what is really needed is effective coordination of the work through the instrumentality of a high grade official who would occupy in the Prime Minister's office a posi-

Supply-Prime Minister's Office
tion very similar to that of deputy minister in the offices of other ministers. I need not point out that for years past, in addition to the work of his own office, the Prime Minister has been president of the privy council and responsible for the work of the office of the privy council and also for that of the Department of External Affairs, he being as well Secretary of State for External Affairs. The result is that these three offices continuously make their demands upon his time. In addition, the Prime Minister has his duties in parliament, and duties connected therewith. Hon. members know how considerable is the time which he must necessarily give to the work of parliament apart altogether from departmental duties, and obligations as the leader of a political party as well as those of Prime Minister apart altogether from parliament. There is need of some one or more persons in the nature of liaison officers to effect contacts between different departments of government and the Prime Minister as well as between parliament and the Prime Minister. These functions cannot be performed by private secretaries who have other equally important duties. I imagine the amount of correspondence to be dealt with and the number of interviews are far beyond the imagination of most hon. members. The work of correspondence alone has come now to where it has to be organized almost as a separate department of government. Perhaps my right hon. friend opposite would give the committee some indication of what he knows has to be oc-complished. I must say to hon. members it will be impossible at all satisfactorily to carry on public work unless the Prime Minister can be supplied with efficient help.
Yesterday we had before us a bill for the appointment of an economic council to advise the Prime Minister. When in opposition I took the stand that an economic council was not what was required in association with the Prime Minister's office; I said that what he required was the services of two or three highly trained experts who could be helpful in preparing material on economic and financial questions, whose services he could command and who could supply him with necessary data when he had to consider any particular subject either for discussion in parliament or in connection with matters of a departmental nature. That I believe is very necessary. This vote is intended to enable a prime minister to retain the services of expert persons to assist in the work of the office. In a general way I believe I have described its purpose.

I do not think any
language the Prime Minister can use would be an exaggeration of the condition to which he has referred. I am not certain, but I think he will find that in the five years he has been away the correspondence in the office has doubled. I think that is not too strong a statement to make; in times of depression, particularly, that is true. I can only say that I should think it questionable whether the sum was sufficient for the purposes required. There is not any doubt in the world that whoever happens to be Prime Minister in these days, and is at the same time Secretary of State for External Affairs, as the statute requires, and president of the privy council, which it does not require, but which the Prime Minister more or less should be, in order that he may be familiar with what goes on in the various departments of the public service, has no time for reflection and little or no time to consider carefully, as he should, matters affecting large problems of policy. He must go continuously from one thing to another, without having any opportunity to pause and rest, or even to meditate, except the opportunity he may have as he talks to himself walking up the hill, and has a meeting of the cabinet as it were, or something of that kind. Under those circumstances of course the situation is entirely different. However, apart from such cabinet meetings he gets very little opportunity. I assume that possibly the question of under secretaries and other matters enters into this. It may be that the amount is not adequate for the purposes intended. If the country expects any man to serve it as faithfully as one holding the position of prime minister ought to do, he should be provided with the instrumentalities to enable him to do so. Certainly they have not existed to the extent all of us would like, because of the general view held by the public that there is no necessity to spend .money in the office, and that there are enough people around there to look after the job, and all that sort of thing, without pausing for a moment to realize just what is involved.
I congratulate the first minister upon having in the estimates a provision which I hope will have the effect he suggests it will, namely, that of coordinating the efforts of the three departments over which at the present moment the Prime Minister presides. One of my colleagues has suggested that it is his view that it would be in the public interest, in the long run, if the offices of Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs were separated. On the
Supply-Prime Minister's Office

other hand, as it now reads the statute provides that, for reasons that are obvious, the Secretary of State for External Affairs shall be the Prime Minister. I believe that was the view accepted by all overseas dominions, and I think the reasons are quite apparent to all. I assure the committee that from my observations this amount will not be more than adequate to enable sufficient assistance to be provided the Prime Minister in order that he may properly discharge the very onerous duties of his office.
If I may refer to the fact, may I say that with respect to the economic council there seemed to be an entire misunderstanding in what was said last evening. It was intended that the Prime Minister, by referring matters to the economic council, might receive reports which would enable him, after examination, to determine the best course of action to follow. In no sense could the council be said to be set up to take the place of cabinet ministers. They, with the Prime Minister, must take the final action upon questions affecting matters of policy. The council were only to provide information to enable the ministers to determine what action should be taken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I thank
my right hon. friend for his kindness in giving the committee the information he has with respect to what he knows so well to be the work of the office of the Prime Minister, combined with the other offices he has mentioned. May I say to him that his observations about correspondence, and the work in connection therewith having doubled since I was in office five years ago, are perfectly true. Not only has the correspondence more than doubled, but the intricacy of the questions which have to be dealt with has increased to a degree that I had not believed possible. I must say that in three directions in particular I notice a tremendous increase in the volume of work. One has already been mentioned by the former Prime Minister, the exacting and trying work that arises out of a period of depression. The load in that regard falls very very heavily on a Prime Minister's back. Appeals in this connection are made direct to him from a multitude of directions, and he is responsible for discussing with his colleagues all phases of legislation in connection therewith.
Another question concerning which there has been a great increase in correspondence, and great difficulty in dealing with it, is the whole subject of trade. These communications come directly to the Prime Minister's office in a way they never did formerly.
I guess it is a habit they got from the time I was Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am afraid
that a number of departments have got into the habit of waiting for some word from the Prime Minister. I have not said anything about the matter, but there is no doubt about that.
The willing horse.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Much has been said about economic nationalism as it obtains in different countries of the world. That wretched policy has done more I think to add cares and worry to government departments than has all the mass of other things put together because it raises endless questions of the effects of quotas, restrictions, and the like, which are an entirely new phenomenon. At any rate they did not present themselves when I occupied the office of Prime Minister previously. To-day in a multitude of directions correspondence arises from them. They serve to beget endless friction and to arouse all kinds of antagonisms, the effects of these find their way sooner or later to the Prime Minister's office.
Get rid of them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They cannot,
I believe, be got rid of too quickly, but to rid the world of them will require time. The world has changed and countries, too, in their relations with each other, and these changes have to be taken into account.
The third change, and perhaps the most serious of all, is the extent to which the time of the Prime Minister, acting more particularly as Secretary of State for External Affairs, is taken up with all important External Affairs matters. I need only mention the correspondence that has come in during the last few months from Geneva, and from London; the correspondence that has developed with respect to the situation as it is in Europe. Whether one were himself Secretary of State for External Affairs or whether that portfolio were held by a separate member of the cabinet, I do not see how the Prime Minister could escape having to go through the despatches which deal with foreign affairs in a world of the character in which we live to-day. I notice there, as well, a tremendous change. Our country is being drawn into international situations to a degree that I myself think is alarming. That is something to which I hope, as we go along, we shall get a chance to give much more thought and attention.
Personally nothing would please me more than to have one of my colleagues administer the Department of External Affairs as a scpa-

Supply-Prime Minister's Office
rate department of government, and leave me with the office of Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council. When, however, I have discussed the question with my colleagues, and when I have thought it over myself, it really has seemed that in the long run less difficulty and possible confusion would arise and less time be lost if for a while at least matters were to be carried on as they are. However, so to do will require giving to the Prime Minister the right to obtain from time to time the services of men who have expert knowledge of these questions. What I should say, the public does not appreciate, were I for a moment to think that there could be any criticism of expenditure on this score, is the extent to which the class of questions which governments and parliaments are called upon to deal with to-day, and which the Prime Minister has to deal with, in larger variety perhaps than any other of the ministers, demands special training, knowledge and study. They are not matters on which a private secretary can be expected to inform or advise his chief. They are matters that require careful thought and study and sound and sure advice. The additional amount that has been asked for and which the committee seems prepared to grant in a ready way, is for the purpose of making it possible to obtain from time to time this sort of assistance.

I just wish to say one
word, Mr. Chairman. I do not know any method by which the Prime Minister can escape from reading the dispatches which come to the office of external affairs. I remember Mr. MacDonald telling me that he frequently had to sit up until the early hours of the morning to read the dispatches from the foreign office, for he said it was a rule that he had made, and which he believed his predecessors had followed, that the Prime Minister should read every dispatch that came through the foreign office. Great Britain sends to us cables with respect to matters that affect the welfare of the overseas dominions and even with respect to matters in which they might be only indirectly interested. The result is that when they are decoded and prepared for submission to whoever happens to be minister for external affairs it takes a long time to read them, and one has to discuss them with his colleagues. It frequently happens that two or three matters all of first rate importance come to the attention of the minister in a single day. How on earth a man is going to be able to carry on the burden of first minister when he has at the same time to keep in his mind everything affecting ques-12739-42
tions raised by cablegrams from various parts of the world, I do not know. For instance, this very Japanese situation which has arisen in the last few days has no doubt resulted in the receipt of cables from London on the one hand, and from Tokyo on the other, and one has to make up one's mind on these matters. It is true that the permanent officials of the department are excellently qualified for the positions which they occupy. One hesitates to say this in the presence of the under-Secretary, but he has had wide experience and an excellent training, and he brings to bear on all these questions an understanding which would not be that of the average man. Nevertheless the fact remains that he is overworked.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

How it is possible to
carry on that office without extra assistance, I do not know, and I doubt very much whether the sum mentioned will get the expert opinion or advice that the Prime Minister should receive from time to time. Compare conditions to-day with what they were not so very long ago. For instance, in Lord Salisbury's time he used to write very important dispatches with his own hand. It is recorded that the dispatch that was written on the Behring sea matter to Mr. Blaine was written in Lord Salisbury's own hand. He used to write his dispatches at Hatfield over the week-end. Lord Curzon also wrote some of his dispatches.
In these days the system is a very simple one. When a dispatch reaches the minister for foreign affairs it has passed through the hands of highly trained men; in fact, they know much more about the subject, apart altogether from questions of policy, than does their chief. We have not yet developed in this country that reservoir of highly qualified men such as they have in a country like Great Britain. For instance, when they set up their tariff board they simply had to select this man, that man and another man, and they got the most highly trained and the most efficient men in the kingdom. We have not yet done that in this country, and I have always felt that the rewards in mere money are not at all adequate for the services rendered. That was one of the reasons I always had in mind why there should be some other reward than that of mere money. People sometimes speak of it as honours or recognition of merit, but it becomes a very powerful factor in determining the action of permanent public officials. The late Mr. Kipling pointed that out in one of his stories. He pointed out that very frequently in India



Supply-Prime Minister's Office
the struggle between whether it should be a C.I.E. or a C.S.I. had much to do with the zeal and determination with which men threw themselves into their work. That looks like a very small thing, but the fact is that if we are to get that kind of trained public servants who will make a career of their work as they do in Great Britain, we have in every sense to magnify the importance' of their position and give them every possible support, attracting, by salaries that are at least in some sense adequate, the best possible men that may foe available for that purpose. A new country finds it difficult sometimes to understand that, but it is money well spent, and even in times of depression you have to pay men fairly well or they leave the service and are taken into private enterprise. That has happened and I suppose will continue to happen. It has happened occasionally in Great Britain; it has happened here and will happen in other countries. But certainly, in the office of Prime Minister, I cannot too strongly suggest to the committee that some provision must be made that will enable whoever is there to have at least a little freedom from toil, for meditation and thought, with the assurance that the work will not be neglected and that the best possible brain is giving its attention to providing a solution of the particular problems with which a Prime Minister has to deal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I cannot allow what my right hon. friend has just said to go by without expressing to him my very warm appreciation for having stated what he alone can say with more authority perhaps than anyone else in the house. What I should like to point out to hon. members, because we are' considering this matter now in its many aspects, is this: Hon. members see a Prime Minister in the house; they see that he has to foe here practically every afternoon and evening, or at least somewhere about the buildings. They forget, however, that the time thus spent does not represent his work at all; his work has to be done apart from the time he spends in the House of Commons in the afternoon and at night. Members perhaps forget that a meeting of the cabinet has to be held every day, and that Saturdays, which are more or less free days to others, are really the only days on which the cabinet can find opportunity for maturing policies, reviewing legislation and the like. These many demands leave only the forenoons for the Prime Minister to do the real work of his office, and departments for which he is responsible, the class of work to which the leader of the opposition has just referred.

Unless a man in the responsible position of Prime Minister can have at his side those on whose ability he can completely rely, he cannot begin to do his duty either to the House of Commons or to the country. I thank my right hon. friend again for his assistance in helping to have this understood.

As one who a few minutes ago urged that some of the advertising abroad be cut down, may I say that I heartily appreciate the position as outlined by the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition. As a private member, I do not think that the office can be too fully organized or that we can take too great pains in securing a large number of trained men for positions of this character. I have sometimes thought that the Department of External Affairs, in the last year or two, has been called upon altogether too much to do all sorts of odd jobs, as for example on various commissions. We ought to have a very much larger number of men with wide economic training who would foe capable of handling economic and international affairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for what he has just said.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:

Supply-A griculture-Pub licity

What is the publicity of this department? I confess that during my little experience I found it difficult to ascertain how every department could have a publicity bureau of its own, and I could never find out why it was not possible to correlate the efforts and direct them under one head as is now done with our advertising in Great Britain. That is all I desire to say.

The publicity of the department is largely a matter of getting out publications that indicate to farmers in different parts of Canada what is being done in these various branches. Periodicals are sent here and there throughout Canada giving information with regard to the findings of the different branches in their research work and in other connections.

The real difficulty which I found-and I was not able in the limited time at my disposal to deal with it, for the reasons I have given-was the competition between departments to secure information and give it to the public. The competition between the bureau of statistics, for instance, and the Department of National Revenue with respect to what the revenue was for the preceding month is always, to me, rather interesting. It is really a difference between Trade and Commerce on the one hand and National Revenue on the other, and the minister knows better than I the difficulties in connection with the competition between the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce. When I saw the increase in this item I wondered why there should be an increase in publicity and extension, because the mere increase in the publication of reports simply means the waste in many instances of additional sums for paper and ink, because the extent to which they are read is, I am sorry to say, very limited.
Not read at all.

ties are much nearer the ordinary farmers and ought to be able to undertake a great deal of the distribution end of these matters. There is a vast amount of duplication. I should like to ask the minister if there is any possibility of closer coordination.

But there are people in every community who do read one or another of these periodicals, and whenever a farmers' gathering is held, while perhaps nine out of ten of the people who are there have never read them and have never seen them, one individual may and on many occasions does get up and give the information to those who are present, and they get it sometimes in spite of themselves. that was obtained in Saskatchewan last year by these men for their seed was fifteen cents a bushel above the market price of wheat, which is not a very considerable amount, or anything that I think anyone would complain about. I believe any farmer would prefer to buy that kind of seed from men with a reputation that most of these men have for the production of good seed, rather than pay the market price for seed of which they knew little or nothing.

The explanation given
by the minister would seem to be reasonable. I was just asking my colleagues if they could tell who it was who raised the issue. I recall making a mental note to try to ascertain the facts. I think the hon. member who raised the question is not at present in the chamber. At that time I believe he sat to the left of the Speaker, and I was much taken with what he said. There are many men in the west who have taken high honours for producing high class seed. Very few of these men have made much money for themselves at that work. Just a little while ago the review board of Saskatchewan was meeting in Saskatoon and one of the most prominent of these seed growers, one who had taken many honours, came before them hopelessly involved because he was not able to make enough on his farming operations to carry on. There are many such men in the different provinces, and I do not think any of them have made much out of the high class seed they have produced. The price at times does seem high to farmers who have to buy the seed, but if we take into consideration the amount of work, the care in growing and cleaning and keeping the seed separate and all that kind of thing, as well as the cost of buying seed originally, the net results are not very large. But these men take pride in their work and pleasure in carrying on that type of seed selection and reproduction, and they keep on doing this as long as they can. I think that is the history of a great many seed growers in western Canada who have achieved prominence; they have not gained much wealth for themselves. The result for their neighbours has been valuable. The seed is moved from one district to another readily and cheaply in small quantities. When these men hold a supply of good seed available, farmers hundreds of miles away are able to
get supplies which might cost fairly high per unit, but the aggregate cost of which is small. I believe the work should be encouraged.

Total Subventions Available to a Province
1.	The total subvention available to a province within the dominion fiscal year shall not exceed the sum of $1,200 unless more than one million acres are under cultivation in field crops within the province, in which case the subvention may be increased pro rata $1,200 for each additional million acres under cultivation a9 reported by the Dominion Bureau of Statsties for the previous year, provided that the total subvention shall not exceed $1,200 pro rata per hundred thousand of total population as shown by the latest available federal census return.
2.	These subventions shall be for the purposes and in the amounts hereinafter specified, but shall not exceed one-half the total amounts paid as cash prizes or grants by the provincial Departments of Agriculture.
